title: Slam Dunk
synopsis: A delinquent joins his school basketball team to impress a girl and discovers he is good at it, in the series that made basketball popular in Japan. Filed under 5, the turn.
body:
5Reduced, this title gives 5. It sits on The Turn with the rest of a turn.

What it is

Takehiko Inoue's Slam Dunk ran in Weekly Shonen Jump from 1990 to 1996. Hanamichi Sakuragi, a tall, aggressive and academically hopeless first-year, joins the basketball club for entirely the wrong reasons and turns out to have genuine physical gifts and no idea how to use them.

Why it is held up as the model sports manga

The sport is real. Inoue depicts basketball accurately enough that the games are followable as basketball, with legible court geometry, plausible tactics and specific skills. The reader learns the sport as Sakuragi does.

The protagonist's ignorance is the engine. Because Sakuragi knows nothing, explanation is natural rather than intrusive, and his incremental competence is measurable — the story can show progress in terms of a rebound taken correctly rather than an abstract power increase.

It refuses easy triumph. The series is notably willing to let its team lose, and its ending is admired precisely for declining the sweep that the format invites.

Its influence

Slam Dunk is widely credited with a substantial increase in basketball's popularity in Japan, which is an unusually concrete cultural effect for a comic. Within the medium it set the standard sports manga template: a novice lead, a demanding coach, a rival school, and technical explanation woven through competition.

Reading it

Completed, self-contained, and one of the most reliable recommendations for readers indifferent to sport — the actual subject is obsession and the gap between talent and skill.

How the story is divided

Hanamichi Sakuragi, a delinquent who joins Shohoku High's basketball team to impress a girl, learns the game from nothing. The first part builds the team and its rivalries through a practice match against Ryonan. The middle covers the Inter-High prefectural tournament, against Kainan, Shoyo and Ryonan. The last part takes Shohoku to the national tournament and a match against Sannoh, the best team in the country, that many readers consider the finest game in sports manga.

Adaptations

Toei's anime (1993–1996) ended before the national tournament. In 2022 Takehiko Inoue wrote and directed The First Slam Dunk, an animated film that adapts the Sannoh match from the point of view of the point guard, Ryota Miyagi.

Reading it today

Complete in 31 volumes, it is one of the best sports manga to start with. The television anime stops after the prefectural tournament, so readers who know it should read on from there.

title: Solo Leveling
altTitles: Ore dake Level Up na Ken
synopsis: The weakest hunter in the world gains the ability to level up like a video game character, and stops being weak. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3Reduced, this title gives 3. It sits on The Telling with the rest of an act of telling.

What it is

Solo Leveling is a Korean webtoon, not a manga. It adapts Chugong's web novel and was drawn by Jang Sung-rak, who worked under the name DUBU. It ran on KakaoPage and Piccoma from 2018 to 2021. Gates to monster-filled dungeons have opened worldwide, and awakened humans called hunters clear them for money. Sung Jinwoo is ranked at the bottom until a dungeon nearly kills him and a system only he can see offers him quests.

Why it is here

It is included in this reference because it is one of the works most responsible for pushing Korean webtoons into the same conversation as manga for English-language readers, and because the format difference is instructive. Webtoons are drawn for vertical scrolling on a phone: full colour, one image column, pacing controlled by how far you scroll rather than by page turns. A reveal is timed by empty space, not by a page break.

What it does well

The art is the draw. Jang Sung-rak's rendering is dense and cinematic, and the shadow army sequences in the later half are genuinely spectacular pieces of colour composition. He died in 2022 at 37; the work is widely regarded as the high-water mark for the medium's action illustration.

What kind of story it is

Structurally it is a power fantasy and does not pretend otherwise. Jinwoo gets stronger, the opposition scales, and the pleasure is the escalation itself. Characterisation is thin and the supporting cast largely exists to react to him. Read on those terms it is extremely effective; read expecting the interiority of the seinen titles elsewhere in this wiki, it will disappoint.

Terminology note

Korean comics are manhwa; Chinese are manhua. Vertical-scroll digital comics from any country are webtoons. The terms overlap and are frequently used loosely.

How the story is divided

The story begins with Jinwoo as the weakest hunter, nearly killed in a double dungeon, and his reawakening with the System. It follows his secret rise through ever harder gates, his job-change quest and the shadow army it gives him, and the raids that make his name, including the infestation of Jeju Island by monstrous ants. In the final arcs, the dungeons are revealed as part of a war between rulers far beyond the human world, and the story ends with an epilogue.

Adaptations and sequel

A-1 Pictures' anime (2024) was a worldwide hit, and its second season, Arise from the Shadow, followed in 2025. A sequel webtoon, Solo Leveling: Ragnarok, follows Jinwoo's son; its second season ended in 2026 when its artist began military service.

Reading it today

The original webtoon is complete. Our guide to manga, manhwa and manhua explains how the format differs from manga.

title: Spy x Family
synopsis: A spy assembles a fake family for a mission, not knowing his adopted daughter reads minds and his wife is an assassin. 51 in the letters, reducing to 6.
body:
6The letters of this title total 51, a 6 — the number of care, community, and the weight of duty.

What it is

Tatsuya Endo's Spy x Family began in the digital magazine Shōnen Jump+ in 2019 and is ongoing. Twilight, an intelligence agent in a Cold War pastiche, needs a wife and child within a week to infiltrate an elite school. He adopts Anya, who is telepathic, and marries Yor, who kills people for a living. Nobody tells anybody.

How the comedy works

The premise is a dramatic irony engine. The reader knows all three secrets; each character knows only their own; Anya knows everything and cannot say so. Nearly every joke is generated by that asymmetry, and Endo is disciplined about not resolving it — revelations that other series would spend early are held back for years.

The strip is also unusually well-drawn for a comedy. Endo's previous work was action, and the fight scenes are staged with real weight, which makes the tonal switches land instead of deflating.

What it is about

Under the farce is a straightforward argument that a family built for the wrong reasons can become a real one. All three leads chose this arrangement instrumentally and are, visibly, being changed by it. The series treats Anya's schoolwork with the same seriousness as an assassination, and that flattening is deliberate.

Where it sits

It publishes in Shōnen Jump+, the digital sibling of Weekly Shōnen Jump, on a roughly biweekly schedule rather than weekly. This is why the chapters are longer and more finished-looking than a weekly title's, and why the volume count grows slowly.

The reservation

The episodic structure means the espionage plot advances very slowly, and readers who came for the spy thriller rather than the family comedy tend to lose patience. Yor is also written more narrowly than the other two leads, though later arcs correct this.

How the story is divided

Much of the series is self-contained missions and school episodes: Anya's entrance exam for Eden Academy, her attempts to earn Stella stars, a dodgeball match and a family vacation. Longer arcs are woven between them: Yor's assassination assignment on a luxury cruise, a hijacking of Anya's school bus, and a long flashback into Loid's childhood in wartime. The spy plot, Operation Strix, advances slowly underneath.

Adaptations

Wit Studio and CloverWorks' anime began in 2022, with a second season in 2023 and a third in 2025, and the original film Spy x Family Code: White (2023) sends the family on a winter holiday.

Reading it today

The episodic structure makes it easy to read a volume at a time. Readers who know the anime will find the manga further ahead, published roughly twice a month on Shōnen Jump+.

title: The Apothecary Diaries
synopsis: A pharmacist sold into service at an imperial rear palace solves poisonings and court intrigues while trying to avoid promotion. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3The letters of this title total 102, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

What it is

The Apothecary Diaries began as Natsu Hyūga's web novel and has been adapted into two concurrent manga versions. The one drawn by Nekokurage has run in Monthly Big Gangan since 2017 and is the more widely translated. Maomao, an apothecary from the pleasure district, is kidnapped and sold as a servant into the emperor's rear palace, where she cannot stop herself from diagnosing things.

How it works

It is a procedural. Most chapters present a problem — an illness, a poisoning, an inexplicable death, a rumour — and Maomao resolves it through pharmacology and observation. The solutions are usually material: lead in cosmetics, mercury, a misidentified plant, a dietary deficiency. The series is genuinely interested in the chemistry and takes time to explain it.

Around the cases runs a slower political plot about succession, and the two layers intersect more often as the series goes on.

The setting

The court is a fictionalised imperial China rather than a historical one. The rear palace — thousands of consorts and servants in an enclosed hierarchy — functions as a closed-room setting where information is currency and nobody can leave. That constraint is what makes the mysteries work.

What it is about

Maomao is a rare protagonist: openly uninterested in romance, motivated primarily by curiosity, and inclined to test poisons on herself. Her refusal to be elevated is the running joke and also the argument — the series is about a woman with expertise navigating a system that only values her as an ornament, and it lets her win by being useful in ways the system cannot classify.

Which version to read

The Nekokurage adaptation is more atmospheric and better paced. A second manga adaptation drawn by Minoji Kurata exists and is closer to the novel's detail. The light novels are the original and go further than either.

How the story is divided

The series moves from the rear palace, where Maomao serves a consort and solves the mysteries around her, to the outer court, where she works for the eunuch Jinshi and investigates poisonings and accidents that turn out to be connected. As it continues, the cases build into a conspiracy against the imperial family and a rebellion, and Maomao's own background, as the daughter of a strategist and a courtesan, comes into play.

Adaptations

The anime by OLM and TOHO Animation Studio began in 2023, and its second season aired in two parts in 2025.

Reading it today

The manga adaptations are still running and follow the novels at a distance. Readers who want the whole story ahead of the anime should go to the light novels.

title: Tower of God
synopsis: A boy enters a tower that grants any wish at its summit, chasing the girl who left him behind to climb it. 56 in the letters, reducing to 11.
body:
11The letters of this title total 56, an 11 — the number of inspiration, tension, and heightened awareness.

What it is

Tower of God is a Korean webtoon by the artist known as SIU, serialised on Naver Webtoon since 2010 and still running. Bam follows Rachel into a tower whose climbers are promised anything they want at the top, and is admitted as an irregular — someone who forced the door rather than being chosen.

The structure

Each floor is a test, and the tests are the point. They are built as puzzles with explicit rules, and the solutions turn on cooperation, betrayal, or an unstated assumption in the rules themselves. The series runs on the tension between the tower's meritocratic promise and the fact that it is administered by families who arrived first.

The cast is enormous and the worldbuilding is dense to the point of obstruction. Positions, shinsu, ranking systems, and administrator hierarchies are introduced faster than they are explained, and the series expects readers to accumulate understanding rather than be taught.

The art

Early Tower of God is drawn crudely — SIU began as an amateur and the first season looks it. The improvement across a decade of weekly output is one of the most visible artist-development arcs in webtoons, and readers routinely warn newcomers to push through the first fifty episodes.

What it is about

Ambition and what it costs the people it climbs over. Rachel's choice, made in the first episode and re-examined for a decade, is the moral core: the series is unusually willing to let a character be small, resentful, and unredeemed. Bam's arc is the mirror — someone with overwhelming power who keeps choosing attachment over ascent.

The reservation

It is very long, structurally sprawling, and has significant pacing problems in its middle seasons. It is a substantial commitment and openly unfinished.

title: Vagabond
synopsis: A fictionalised account of the swordsman Miyamoto Musashi, following a violent young man's long attempt to become something other than a killer. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3Title sums to 30 and reduces to 3 — The Telling, where the reference files an act of telling.

What it is

Takehiko Inoue's Vagabond began in 1998 and is an adaptation of Eiji Yoshikawa's novel about Miyamoto Musashi, the historical swordsman. It follows Musashi from a brutal youth through years of duels and self-imposed training.

The art

This is the work Inoue is most admired for technically. He moved substantially toward brush and ink, and the later volumes in particular achieve a looseness and weight that reads closer to traditional painting than to conventional manga rendering.

The style is doing thematic work. Precision in the early volumes gives way to something more gestural as the story becomes less interested in swordsmanship and more interested in what a life of it costs.

What it is about

The duels are not the point. Vagabond is a study of a man attempting to become strong and slowly discovering that strength as he understood it is not worth having. Long stretches concern farming, teaching, and sitting still, and these are treated as more consequential than the fights.

Its parallel narrative following a second swordsman offers a deliberate contrast — a person with far more natural facility and far less capacity to change.

Its status

The series has been on extended hiatus, with Inoue having spoken publicly about the difficulty of continuing it. It should be approached as unfinished and possibly permanently so, which is a genuine loss given how close the source material's ending is.

How the story is divided

The first volumes follow Takezō, later Musashi, from the battle of Sekigahara to his fight with the Yoshioka school in Kyoto. His training with the spear masters of the Hōzōin and with Yagyū Sekishūsai follows. A long middle section turns to Sasaki Kojirō, here a deaf swordsman, and tells his life from childhood. The latest volumes follow Musashi to a village where he farms and learns, far from duels.

Publication and recognition

Thirty-seven volumes were published before the series went on hiatus in 2015. It won the Kodansha Manga Award in 2000 and the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize in 2002, and has sold more than 82 million copies.

Reading it today

Read it knowing that it stops. Our entry on Takehiko Inoue covers Slam Dunk and Real.

title: Vinland Saga
synopsis: A Viking boy raised on revenge grows into a man who renounces violence entirely, in a historical epic that turns from war story into something considerably stranger. Read from the turn, as a 5.
body:
5Five — change. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Makoto Yukimura's Vinland Saga ran in Monthly Afternoon from 2005 to 2025 and is complete in 29 volumes. It is set in eleventh-century northern Europe, drawing on real history and on Norse sagas. Thorfinn, whose father is killed by a mercenary leader, spends his youth serving that same man while waiting for a chance at revenge.

The turn that defines it

The series is notable for a structural decision most action manga would not attempt. Having spent a long opening act establishing a revenge narrative, it abandons it — and the remainder concerns a protagonist attempting to live without violence in a world organised around it.

This is far more difficult to dramatise than combat, and it is the reason the series is held in the regard it is. The question shifts from whether Thorfinn can win to whether a person who has done what he has done can build anything worth having.

The historical setting

Yukimura works with real events, figures and political structures, and the research is visible in the depiction of ships, farming, slavery and the mechanics of raiding. The violence is not stylised — it is administrative and grim, which supports rather than contradicts the eventual argument.

Reading it

The early volumes are considerably more conventional than what follows, and readers who bounce off the opening as a standard Viking action story are frequently reacting to something the series is deliberately setting up in order to reject. It is seinen and is unsparing throughout.

How the story is divided

The story falls into clear stages. The opening arc, roughly volumes 1–8, follows the boy Thorfinn among Askeladd's mercenaries during the Danish wars for England and the rise of Prince Canute. The Farmland arc, which follows, is quieter: Thorfinn is enslaved on a Danish farm and has to face what he has done. Later arcs take him back to Iceland, east across the Baltic, and finally west to Vinland, the land across the ocean, to try to build a settlement without war.

History behind it

The title and the ending come from the Icelandic Vinland sagas, which tell of Norse voyages to North America around 1000 AD, and the real Thorfinn Karlsefni, who led an attempt to settle there. Canute is the historical king who ruled England, Denmark and Norway. Our guide to manga set in history outside Japan has more historical manga.

Adaptations

Wit Studio's first anime season (2019) covered the opening arc, and MAPPA's second (2023) adapted the Farmland arc faithfully.

title: Yotsuba&!
synopsis: A small adopted girl encounters ordinary things — a swing, a bicycle, rain — for the first time, in a comedy about noticing the world. The title reduces to 22 — the edifice.
body:
22A 22 by its title: master builder (22), and therefore the edifice.

What it is

Kiyohiko Azuma's Yotsuba&! began in 2003 and follows Yotsuba, a five-year-old girl living with her adoptive father, as she moves to a new neighbourhood and encounters entirely unremarkable things with complete astonishment.

There is no plot. Chapters concern a cicada, a bicycle, a typhoon, a trip to buy milk.

Why it works

The premise is a device for restoring attention. Because Yotsuba has no context for anything, ordinary objects and events are presented as genuinely novel, and the reader is invited to look at them properly.

Azuma's comic timing is exceptionally precise. The humour depends almost entirely on panel rhythm — a pause held one beat longer than expected, a reaction placed after the page turn — which makes it a good demonstration of how much comedy in comics is structural rather than verbal.

The art

Deceptively plain and technically excellent. Backgrounds are detailed and consistent, giving the neighbourhood a real geography, and this grounding is what makes Yotsuba's astonishment land. Her expressions are the other achievement — extremely simple linework producing an unusually wide emotional range.

What it is not

It is not sentimental about childhood, and it does not build toward anything. The adults are competent and unremarkable, the situations are small, and nothing is at stake. Readers wanting narrative momentum should look elsewhere; readers wanting to feel better are well served.

Who's who

Yotsuba lives with her adoptive father, Koiwai, a translator. Their neighbours are the three Ayase sisters, Asagi, Fūka and Ena, and their mother; Ena's friend Miura; Koiwai's tall friend Jumbo; and Yanda, a part-timer whom Yotsuba considers her enemy. Ena and Miura's cardboard robot, Danbo, became a famous figure in its own right.

Publication and recognition

The series appears slowly, at a volume every few years, and had reached 16 volumes. It won the Grand Prize of the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize in 2016, and has more than 13 million copies in print in Japan. No anime has been made.

Reading it today

Start at volume 1 and read in order, since Yotsuba's summer passes in real time. Our guide to slice of life and iyashikei places it among quiet manga, and our entry on Azumanga Daioh covers Azuma's first series.

title: Azumanga Daioh
synopsis: Four-panel strips following a group of high-school girls and their teachers through three years of school, in a comedy built almost entirely on timing. 58 in the letters, reducing to 4.
body:
4The letters of this title total 58, a 4 — the number of structure, labour, and the building of lasting systems.

What it is

Kiyohiko Azuma's Azumanga Daioh ran in MediaWorks' Dengeki Daioh from 1999 to 2002 and was collected in four volumes. It follows a handful of students, among them a ten-year-old prodigy skipped ahead into high school, and two of their teachers across three school years, from entrance to graduation.

How it is built

The whole series is yonkoma: four-panel strips, each complete in itself. There is no plot beyond the passing of the school calendar, sports days, cultural festivals, summer trips and exams. What carries it is timing: the third panel sets up an expectation, and the fourth declines to meet it in a way that is exactly in character.

Why it matters

It showed how much a four-panel comedy could hold. Because the strips follow the same cast through three years that really pass, and end at graduation, small running jokes accumulate into something closer to a portrait of a class. The 2002 anime adaptation brought it to a wide audience outside Japan.

What followed

A long line of school comedies about a small group of friends and their daily routine, told in or inspired by the four-panel format, trace back to it. Azuma's next series, Yotsuba&!, kept the attention to ordinary moments and moved to full-page chapters.

Who's who

The students are Chiyo, the ten-year-old genius; Osaka, a transfer student from Osaka who is slow, dreamy and philosophical; Tomo, loud and reckless; Yomi, her sensible friend; Sakaki, tall, silent and secretly in love with cute things; and Kagura, the sporty rival who joins in the second year. Their teachers are Yukari, the irresponsible English teacher, and Nyamo, her more sensible friend and rival from the PE department.

Adaptations

J.C.Staff's anime (2002) adapted the whole manga in 26 episodes. A new edition in 2009 added extra chapters.

title: A Drifting Life
synopsis: Yoshihiro Tatsumi's autobiography in comics: a young artist in postwar Osaka, the rental-book market, and the invention of gekiga. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3The letters of this title total 75, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

What it is

A Drifting Life is Yoshihiro Tatsumi's memoir, drawn over more than a decade, from 1995 to 2006, and collected in 2008 as a book of more than eight hundred pages. Tatsumi appears under a thin fictional name, Hiroshi Katsumi, but the events are his own.

What it covers

The book runs from the end of the Second World War to 1960. It follows a teenager in Osaka who sends strips to magazine competitions, idolises Osamu Tezuka, and begins drawing for the rental-book publishers. Alongside it runs a history of the period: films, strikes, prices and the headlines of each year.

Why it matters

It is the most direct account there is of how gekiga was born. Tatsumi shows the practical reasons behind the movement, from the demands of rental-book publishers to the influence of film, and the moment in 1957 when he chose a new word for what he was drawing.

Recognition

The book won the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize in 2009. Its English edition, published by Drawn & Quarterly in 2009, won two Eisner Awards the following year and did much to introduce Tatsumi to readers outside Japan.

How the book is organised

The chapters move year by year, each opening with the news of the time. They follow Hiroshi's first published strips as a schoolboy, his brother's illness and jealousy, his work for the Osaka rental-book publishers, his move to Tokyo, and the founding of the Gekiga Workshop with fellow artists, among them Takao Saitō, who would later create Golgo 13. It ends in 1960, with gekiga established and Hiroshi still uncertain of his own future.

Adaptations

Eric Khoo's animated film Tatsumi (2011) draws on the book and on five of Tatsumi's short stories.

Reading it today

It is long but easy to read. Our glossary entry on gekiga explains the movement it describes, and our entry on Yoshihiro Tatsumi covers his short stories.

title: Astro Boy
synopsis: A robot boy built by a grieving scientist becomes a hero in a future where robots and humans have not yet agreed on what they owe each other. Filed under 7, the inquiry.
body:
7Title sums to 34 and reduces to 7 — The Inquiry, where the reference files an open question.

What it is

Osamu Tezuka's Astro Boy ran in Kobunsha's monthly magazine Shōnen from 1952 to 1968. Its hero, Atom, is a robot built by Dr. Tenma in the image of his dead son and later rejected by him. Taken in by the kindly Professor Ochanomizu, Atom uses his strength, his jet-powered flight and his capacity for feeling to protect a world that does not fully accept him.

What it is about

Under the adventure plots runs a steady argument about rights. Robots in Astro Boy work, obey and are discarded, and many stories turn on whether a machine that can suffer deserves the protections of a person. Atom is caught between the two sides and belongs fully to neither, which gives the series a melancholy that its bright surface hides.

Why it matters

It is one of the founding works of postwar manga, and its 1963 television adaptation, produced by Tezuka's own studio Mushi Production, was the first weekly half-hour animated series on Japanese television. The low-cost techniques that studio developed to meet a weekly schedule set the economics of television anime for decades.

Its long shadow

Atom's large eyes and rounded design became a template for manga characters, and the robot-as-person question returned throughout Japanese science fiction. Naoki Urasawa's Pluto retells one of its best-known story arcs, "The Greatest Robot on Earth", as an adult mystery.

How to read it

The series is a long run of separate stories, published over sixteen years and collected in many different orders. Among the best known are Atom's birth and rejection by Dr. Tenma; "The Artificial Sun"; and "The Greatest Robot on Earth", in which the robot Pluto destroys the world's most powerful robots one by one. Tezuka often reworked or reordered stories for new editions, and added introductions explaining his changes.

Adaptations

Mushi Production's black-and-white anime (1963–1966) was followed by colour remakes in 1980 and 2003, a computer-animated film (2009) and Naoki Urasawa's Pluto (2003–2009), adapted for Netflix in 2023.

Reading it today

Dark Horse's English edition collects the stories in 23 volumes; any volume can be the first. Our entry on Pluto covers Urasawa's retelling, and our entry on Osamu Tezuka his other works.

title: Black Jack
synopsis: An unlicensed surgeon of impossible skill takes outrageous fees and impossible cases, in short medical stories about what a life is worth. The title reduces to 9 — the closing.
body:
9Filed under 9. The Closing takes a completion, and this entry is hands on one.

What it is

Black Jack ran in Akita Shoten's Weekly Shōnen Champion from 1973 to 1983 and was collected in 25 volumes. Its hero is a scarred surgeon who works without a licence, charges enormous sums and performs operations no one else would attempt. Each chapter is a complete story: a patient, a crisis, an operation and a moral.

How it works

The format suited Tezuka, who had trained and qualified as a physician before committing to manga. The medicine is often fanciful, but the dilemmas are real ones: who gets treated, who pays, when to stop. Black Jack's mercenary pose is usually a front, and many chapters end with him waiving the fee or exposing someone whose motives were worse than his.

Why it matters

It arrived when Tezuka's career was widely thought to be in decline, and its success restored his standing. It also established the medical drama as a manga genre and showed that an anthology of self-contained stories could sustain a weekly series for a decade.

Pinoko

His assistant, Pinoko, a girl assembled by Black Jack from tissue removed from her twin's body, is one of Tezuka's strangest inventions: played for comedy, but rooted in the series' constant question of what counts as a person.

How to read it

There is no order to follow: each chapter stands alone, and Tezuka wrote more than two hundred. A few recur in the series' background: Black Jack's childhood, when a bomb left him nearly dead and he was rebuilt by the surgeon Honma; his search for revenge on those responsible; his half-Japanese skin graft, from a friend who died; and his rival, Dr. Kiriko, who practises euthanasia. These are scattered through the stories rather than told in a single arc.

Adaptations

Osamu Dezaki's OVAs (1993–2011) and film (1996), the television anime (2004–2006) and many live-action versions have been made. Young Black Jack (2011–2019), drawn by other artists, tells his years as a student.

Reading it today

Vertical's English edition collects the stories in 17 volumes. Read a few at random to begin. Our entry on Osamu Tezuka covers his other works.

title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure
altTitles: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険
synopsis: A family saga told in separate parts, each with a new JoJo, a new era and a new kind of fight, built around the visible spirits called Stands. 96 in the letters, reducing to 6.
body:
6The letters of this title total 96, a 6 — the number of care, community, and the weight of duty.

What it is

Hirohiko Araki began JoJo's Bizarre Adventure in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1987. It is structured as a series of parts, each following a different member or incarnation of the Joestar family, from Victorian England to present-day Japan and beyond. The series moved to the monthly Ultra Jump in 2005, during its seventh part, and is still running.

Stands

Its third part introduced the Stand: a fighting spirit with a single, specific ability. Stands turned the series' battles from contests of strength into puzzles. A fight is won by working out what an opponent's power actually does and finding the loophole, and some of the most celebrated battles are fought with abilities that seem useless.

The look

Araki's style is instantly recognisable: poses taken from fashion photography and classical sculpture, sound effects drawn as part of the composition, colour schemes that change from one illustration to the next. The poses became a fan ritual in their own right.

Why it matters

The Stand mechanic became one of the most imitated ideas in shonen manga, the model for countless power systems in which every ability has rules. The series has been running in some form for nearly four decades, and its 2012 anime adaptation brought it a large new international audience.

The parts

The series is divided into parts, each with its own JoJo and its own setting:

  • Phantom Blood (1987): Jonathan Joestar against Dio Brando in Victorian England.
  • Battle Tendency (1987–1989): Joseph Joestar against ancient beings, in 1938.
  • Stardust Crusaders (1989–1992): Jotaro Kujo's journey from Japan to Egypt, and the birth of Stands.
  • Diamond Is Unbreakable (1992–1995): a serial killer in a quiet Japanese town.
  • Golden Wind (1995–1999): Giorno Giovanna in the Italian mafia.
  • Stone Ocean (2000–2003): Jolyne Cujoh in a Florida prison.
  • Steel Ball Run (2004–2011): a horse race across America, in a new continuity.
  • JoJolion (2011–2021) and The JOJOLands (2023–).

Parts 1 to 6 form one continuity; from Part 7 the universe begins again with new versions of familiar names.

Where to start

Start with Part 1: it is short, and the later parts lean on it. Readers who find its 1980s style hard going often start at Part 3, where Stands begin, and go back later. David Production's anime, from 2012, has adapted Parts 1 to 6 faithfully and is an easy way in.

title: Haikyu!!
synopsis: A short boy with an enormous jump joins a fallen high-school volleyball team, in a sports manga about how a team is built. The title reduces to 3 — the telling.
body:
3Filed under 3. The Telling takes an act of telling, and this entry is performs one.

What it is

Haruichi Furudate's Haikyu!! ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2012 to 2020 and was collected in 45 volumes. Shoyo Hinata, too short for the sport he loves, joins Karasuno High's volleyball club, once a contender and now dismissed as "the fallen crows", alongside Tobio Kageyama, a gifted setter nobody wants to play with.

How it works

The series is famous for treating opponents as fully as its heroes. Rival teams get their own histories, their own reasons for playing and their own defeats, and the matches are paced so that every rally has a cost. Hinata and Kageyama's quick attack is the hook, but the subject is the whole team learning how each member's limits can be covered by another.

Why it matters

It renewed the sports manga for its generation, and it is widely credited, along with its anime adaptation, with drawing young people to volleyball in Japan and abroad. It is often recommended as the clearest example of how sports manga turn a tournament into character drama.

The ending

The final arc jumps forward in time to show where the players ended up, a choice that divided readers but completes the series' argument that the high-school years are only one part of a life in sport.

How the story is divided

The story follows Karasuno High's volleyball team through a sequence of tournaments: the team comes together and plays its first practice matches; the Inter-High prefectural qualifiers end in a painful loss; a summer training camp in Tokyo with rival schools remakes the team's attack; the Spring tournament qualifiers build to a final against the powerhouse Shiratorizawa; and the Spring Nationals in Tokyo take up the last third. A time skip at the end follows the players into adulthood.

Adaptations

Production I.G's anime ran for four seasons from 2014 to 2020 and is one of the most admired sports anime. The film Haikyu!! The Dumpster Battle (2024) adapts the long-awaited match against Nekoma.

Reading it today

At 45 volumes it is long, but every tournament is a complete arc. The anime and films reach deep into the Nationals, but the end of the tournament and the epilogue are only in the manga. Our guide to how sports manga work explains why its matches hold up.

title: Delicious in Dungeon
synopsis: Adventurers too broke to buy supplies descend a dungeon by cooking and eating the monsters in it, in a fantasy that takes its own ecology seriously. Filed under 11, the signal.
body:
11The letters of this title total 92, an 11 — the number of inspiration, tension, and heightened awareness.

What it is

Ryoko Kui's Delicious in Dungeon ran in Kadokawa's Harta from 2014 to 2023 and was collected in 14 volumes. When a dragon swallows Laios's sister, his party is left with no money and no supplies. Rather than retreat, they descend the dungeon to rescue her, feeding themselves on the monsters they kill.

How it works

The comedy of cooking a giant scorpion or a walking mushroom is the entry point. Underneath it, Kui works out the dungeon as a functioning ecosystem: what eats what, how a living suit of armour might be built inside, why a monster would evolve the way it has. The recipes come with diagrams.

What it becomes

The series grows steadily darker and stranger. The dungeon has a history, a ruler and a purpose, and the question of what the party will do once they reach Laios's sister turns into one about desire, appetite and the cost of getting what you want.

Why it matters

It is one of the most admired fantasy manga of its decade, praised for the consistency of its world-building and for characters, particularly the obsessive Laios, who are unusually specific. It was voted the top recommended manga in the 2016 edition of Takarajimasha's guide Kono Manga ga Sugoi!, and its 2024 anime adaptation by Studio Trigger broadened its audience considerably.

How the story is divided

When their leader's sister is eaten by a dragon deep in a dungeon, a party of adventurers sets out to rescue her before she is digested, cooking and eating the monsters on the way because they cannot afford supplies. The first half is a descent through the dungeon's floors, one recipe at a time. The second half turns the food logic into something larger, about the dungeon's creator, the demon behind it, and what desire costs.

Adaptations

Studio Trigger's anime (2024) was a worldwide hit on Netflix. A second season is scheduled for October 2027.

Complete in 14 volumes. Every recipe is worked out as if it were real, and the world's ecology is consistent down to the monsters' digestion. Our guide to manga about food and cooking has more in the genre.

title: Kingdom
synopsis: A war orphan sets out to become the greatest general under heaven, in a historical epic about the unification of China by the state of Qin. The title reduces to 1 — the opening.
body:
1A 1 by its title: leader & pioneer, and therefore the opening.

What it is

Yasuhisa Hara's Kingdom has run in Shueisha's Weekly Young Jump since 2006 and passed seventy volumes in the 2020s. It is set in China's Warring States period and follows Xin, a slave boy who wants to become a great general, and Ying Zheng, the young king of Qin who will become the first emperor of a unified China.

How it works

The series is built from battles. Campaigns last for volumes, and Hara treats each as a problem of strategy, morale and command, explaining formations and the decisions of generals at a level of detail rare in manga. Between the wars, palace politics at the Qin court supply a second, quieter kind of conflict.

History and invention

The outline follows the historical record of Qin's wars, and many characters are drawn from it. Where the sources are thin, as they often are, Hara invents freely, so Kingdom is best read as historical fiction on a known scaffold rather than as history.

Why it matters

It is one of the best-selling seinen manga of the century in Japan, won the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize Grand Prize in 2013, and is the clearest current example of the long military epic. Hara worked as an assistant to Takehiko Inoue before his debut, and the attention to physical weight in combat shows it.

How the story is divided

The series moves from war to war. The opening arcs follow Xin from the day he meets the young king through a palace coup and his first battles as a foot soldier. He rises to lead a hundred men, then a thousand, then more, while Ying Zheng secures his throne against rivals at court. Its great set pieces include the coalition of states that invades Qin, the campaign against the city of Ye, and the long wars against Zhao. Each campaign lasts many volumes.

Adaptations

The anime began in 2012 and its sixth season aired in 2025. The live-action films, beginning in 2019, became one of the most successful film series in Japan, with a fifth announced for 2026.

Reading it today

With more than seventy-five volumes, it is a long commitment. Viz Media began an English edition in 2025. Our guide to manga set in history outside Japan discusses how much of it is history.

title: Golden Kamuy
synopsis: A Russo-Japanese War veteran and an Ainu girl hunt for hidden gold in early twentieth-century Hokkaido, chased by soldiers, convicts and a ghost of the Shinsengumi. The title reduces to 11 — the signal.
body:
11Filed under 11. The Signal takes a signal received early, and this entry is sees one.

What it is

Satoru Noda's Golden Kamuy ran in Weekly Young Jump from 2014 to 2022 and was collected in 31 volumes. Saichi Sugimoto, a veteran of the Russo-Japanese War known as "Immortal Sugimoto", hears of a fortune in gold stolen from the Ainu. The map to it was tattooed on the bodies of escaped convicts, and he sets out to find it with Asirpa, an Ainu girl whose father is tied to the gold.

How it works

The series mixes registers freely. A chapter can move from a brutal fight to a detailed account of how to hunt and cook a squirrel to a piece of broad comedy. The cast of rivals, from a renegade army unit to an aged Hijikata Toshizō, gives the treasure hunt the structure of a battle royale.

The Ainu

What set it apart was its portrayal of Ainu culture: language, food, hunting, religious practice and clothing, drawn with care and supervised by the Ainu-language scholar Hiroshi Nakagawa. Asirpa is the series' moral and practical centre rather than a guide for the hero, and for many readers it was a first sustained encounter with Ainu life.

Recognition

It won the Manga Taishō in 2016 and the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize Grand Prize in 2018, and Asirpa was the face of the British Museum's 2019 manga exhibition.

How the story is divided

Just after the Russo-Japanese War, Saichi Sugimoto, a veteran, and Asirpa, a young Ainu girl, hunt for a hoard of stolen Ainu gold whose map is tattooed on the bodies of escaped prisoners. The story is a race between three factions, the pair, a rogue army unit under the unforgettable Lieutenant Tsurumi, and a group led by the samurai Hijikata Toshizō, who has survived long after history says he died. It travels across Hokkaido and into Karafuto, the island of Sakhalin, before a final battle for the gold.

Recognition and adaptations

It won the Manga Taishō in 2016 and the Grand Prize of the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize in 2018, and its depiction of Ainu language and culture was made with expert supervision. The anime ran from 2018 and concluded with its final season in 2026. A live-action film and television drama followed in 2024.

title: Uzumaki
synopsis: A small coastal town is slowly consumed by an obsession with spirals, in Junji Ito's best-known horror work. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3The letters of this title total 30, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

What it is

Junji Ito's Uzumaki ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1998 to 1999 and was collected in three volumes. Kirie Goshima, a high-school girl in the town of Kurouzu-cho, watches her neighbours succumb to the spiral: a man who cannot stop looking at whorls, hair that curls into living coils, people who twist their own bodies into shapes they cannot survive.

How it works

The early chapters are close to self-contained, each a new manifestation of the curse, and each built to a single full-page image that the turn of the page reveals. As the series goes on, the episodes join up, the town begins to cut itself off from the world, and the horror becomes a slow apocalypse.

What makes it frightening

Ito's horror rarely explains itself. The spiral has no motive and no rules a character can learn to escape. What he draws instead is fixation: ordinary people becoming absorbed by a pattern until nothing else matters. His clean, almost calm linework makes the transformations worse, because they are rendered with the same care as a schoolroom.

Why it matters

Uzumaki is the usual starting point for readers coming to Ito, and one of the most widely read horror manga outside Japan. It shows how much of manga horror depends on the page-turn as a device.

How the story is divided

The first volume is a sequence of local horrors: Shūichi's father's obsession, Kirie's hair, a classmate's spiral scar. The second turns stranger, with people slowly becoming snails, a lighthouse, and a hospital where babies are born wrong. The third is the town's collapse, as Kurouzu-cho is cut off by storms, the houses are rebuilt into a spiral maze, and Kirie and Shūichi descend to the town's centre. A nineteenth chapter, "Galaxies", was added to later editions.

Adaptations

Higuchinsky's live-action film (2000) was made before the manga ended and uses its own ending. A four-episode anime in black and white, directed by Hiroshi Nagahama, aired on Adult Swim in 2024.

Complete in three volumes, or one in the omnibus edition. Our entry on Junji Ito covers his other work.

title: Witch Hat Atelier
altTitles: とんがり帽子のアトリエ
synopsis: A girl discovers that magic is not inborn but drawn, and becomes the apprentice of a witch in a world that keeps that secret. 72 in the letters, reducing to 9.
body:
9Reduced, this title gives 9. It sits on The Closing with the rest of a completion.

What it is

Kamome Shirahama's Witch Hat Atelier has run in Kodansha's Monthly Morning Two since 2016. Coco, a tailor's daughter, has always believed that witches are born. When she watches the witch Qifrey cast a spell, she learns that magic is made by drawing glyphs with special ink, and that anyone could do it. Her first attempt goes badly wrong, and she becomes Qifrey's apprentice.

Magic as craft

The series' central idea is that magic is a skill, learned like drawing, with rules, materials and practice. Spells are built from shapes, and Coco's progress is shown through the logic of the glyphs. For a manga drawn with such attention, the metaphor is pointed: the magic is literally made with ink and a pen.

The art

Shirahama came to manga from illustration, including covers for American comics, and the pages draw on European book illustration and engraving as much as on manga convention. Dense, finely hatched panels sit beside wide open spreads, and the costume and architecture are consistently inventive.

Why it matters

It is one of the most admired fantasy manga in English translation and won the Eisner Award for Best U.S. Edition of International Material in the Asia category in 2020. It is a strong recommendation for readers who think manga art has a single look.

How the story is divided

The first volumes follow Coco's apprenticeship with Qifrey and his three other apprentices, Agott, Tetia and Richeh, each struggling with magic in her own way. Their lessons and tests are threatened by the Brimmed Caps, outlaw witches who use forbidden magic on human bodies and who seem to have chosen Coco for their own ends. As it continues, the series uncovers Qifrey's own secret, the history of the Day of the Pact that banned magic for ordinary people, and the price of using it to heal.

Adaptations

Bug Films' anime premiered in April 2026, and a second season has been announced. A spin-off by Hiromi Sato, Witch Hat Atelier Kitchen, about the characters' cooking, began in 2019.

Reading it today

Still running, with 16 volumes and more than 9 million copies by 2026. It won the Eisner in 2020 and the Harvey Award for best manga in 2020 and 2025. Our guide to magic and wizards in manga sets it beside other magic systems.

title: Gintama
synopsis: In an Edo period occupied by aliens, a lazy ex-samurai runs an odd-jobs business, in a comedy that turns serious whenever it chooses. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11Filed under 11. The Signal takes a signal received early, and this entry is intuits one.

What it is

Hideaki Sorachi's Gintama ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2003 to 2018, then concluded in Jump GIGA and the Gintama app in 2019, for a total of 77 volumes. In an alternate Edo, aliens have arrived and banned swords. Gintoki Sakata, a veteran of the lost war against them, now runs an odd-jobs business with two young assistants and lives mostly on sweets and borrowed money.

How it works

Most chapters are comedy: absurd jobs, extended parodies of other Jump series, jokes at the expense of the magazine, the editor and the author himself. Then, without warning, a long arc turns into serious samurai drama about loyalty, grief and the war Gintoki fought, before the comedy returns.

The fourth wall

Few manga have mocked their own medium so openly. Characters complain about pacing, popularity polls and their own designs, and the series treats its status as a weekly Jump manga as material.

Why it matters

It is the model of the gag-and-drama hybrid, and proof that a series can keep both registers alive for fifteen years. Its anime adaptation became famous in its own right for the same mixture.

How the story is divided

For most of its run, Gintama alternates one- and two-chapter comedy episodes with serious arcs a few volumes long. The best known of these include the Benizakura arc, the Yoshiwara in Flames arc, set in an underground red-light district, and the Shogun Assassination arc, which reveals much of Gintoki's past. The series ends with the Silver Soul arc, a war for the fate of Earth that took Sorachi several years and several false endings to finish.

Adaptations

Sunrise's anime ran for 367 episodes from 2006 to 2018, followed by the film Gintama: The Very Final (2021), which adapts the manga's ending. A new film retelling the Yoshiwara arc was released in 2026, and an anime of the spin-off Mr. Ginpachi's Zany Class aired in 2025. Two live-action films (2017 and 2018) were also hits. The manga has passed 73 million copies in circulation.

Reading it today

The early volumes are almost entirely comedy, and many readers start with the anime and move to the manga later. The serious arcs read best in order, since they build on one another.

title: Ghost in the Shell
synopsis: A cyborg officer leads a covert police unit through cybercrime and politics, in a future where the line between a mind and its body has blurred. Filed under 1, the opening.
body:
1Title sums to 73 and reduces to 1 — The Opening, where the reference files a first move.

What it is

Masamune Shirow's Ghost in the Shell ran in Kodansha's Young Magazine Kaizokuban from 1989 to 1990 and was collected in a single volume. Major Motoko Kusanagi, whose body is almost entirely artificial, leads Public Security Section 9, a counter-terrorism unit dealing with hackers who can break into human minds through their cybernetic implants.

How it reads

The manga is denser and more playful than its adaptations. Pages are crowded with technical detail, and Shirow annotates them with margin notes explaining his ideas about networks, politics and engineering. The tone shifts between procedural action, slapstick and philosophical speculation.

The question

The "ghost" is whatever makes a person a person once memory can be edited and the body replaced. The story's climax, an encounter with an artificial intelligence that has emerged from the network, asks whether such a being could be alive, and what a merger between it and a human might mean.

Why it matters

Mamoru Oshii's 1995 film adaptation became one of the most influential animated films ever made and shaped how cyberpunk looked on screen worldwide. The franchise has continued in several anime series, but the manga remains the source of its central ideas.

Sequels

Shirow continued the story in Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface, collected in 2001, about what Kusanagi became after the first book's ending, and in Ghost in the Shell 1.5: Human-Error Processor (2003), which collects shorter Section 9 stories. Both are even denser than the first.

Adaptations

After Oshii's 1995 film and its sequel Innocence (2004), the franchise continued in Stand Alone Complex (2002–2005), Arise (2013–2015), a Hollywood film (2017) and SAC_2045 (2020–2022). The Ghost in the Shell by Science SARU, which aired in 2026, is the first anime to adapt the original manga directly.

Reading it today

The single volume can be read in an evening, but Shirow's notes are part of the experience, so take it slowly. Readers who know only the films will find Kusanagi funnier and less solemn here.

title: Kaguya-sama: Love Is War
altTitles: かぐや様は告らせたい
synopsis: Two proud student council members are in love and refuse to confess, each scheming to make the other say it first. 71 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Reduced, this title gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

What it is

Aka Akasaka's Kaguya-sama: Love Is War began in Miracle Jump in 2015, moved to Weekly Young Jump in 2016 and ended in 2022, collected in 28 volumes. Kaguya Shinomiya, heir to a vast conglomerate, and Miyuki Shirogane, a scholarship student and the council president, are attracted to each other. Each believes that whoever confesses first loses.

How it works

Early chapters are built like strategy games. A trivial event, a shared umbrella, a film ticket, a lunch, becomes a battle of plans and counter-plans, narrated by an over-serious voice and scored with a running tally of who "won". The comedy lies in the gap between the scale of the scheming and the smallness of what is at stake.

How it changes

The series slowly turns into a real romance and a story about the supporting cast's difficulties, including family pressure, loneliness and the cost of pride. By its later arcs, the game has become the thing the characters have to give up.

Why it matters

It is the best-known example of the romantic comedy built on a gimmick that it eventually outgrows, and its anime adaptation was one of the most popular comedies of its years.

How the story is divided

The series began in Miracle Jump in 2015 and moved to Weekly Young Jump the following year. Its first half is mostly self-contained chapters of romantic warfare between Kaguya and Miyuki and the absurd schemes of the student council. Around the school festival, the two finally move towards honesty, and the second half turns to what follows: Kaguya's powerful family, the council members' own stories, and whether the couple can survive the world outside the school.

Adaptations

A-1 Pictures' anime ran for three seasons (2019, 2020 and 2022) and continued with the film The First Kiss That Never Ends (2022). There were also two live-action films.

title: Mushishi
synopsis: A wandering specialist treats illnesses caused by mushi, primitive life forms most people cannot see, in quiet episodes set in rural Japan. 43 in the letters, reducing to 7.
body:
7The letters of this title total 43, a 7 — the number of analysis, secrecy, and the search for truth.

What it is

Yuki Urushibara's Mushishi ran from 1999 to 2008, first in a seasonal special issue of Kodansha's Afternoon and then in the monthly magazine itself, and was collected in ten volumes. Ginko, a white-haired man who attracts mushi, travels the countryside of a Japan that resembles the late Edo or Meiji period, helping people whose troubles come from these creatures.

The mushi

Mushi are not monsters. They are closer to the root of life, simpler than plants or animals, and they behave according to their nature rather than with intent. When they harm people, it is usually by accident, and Ginko's solutions are those of a doctor or naturalist, not an exorcist. Some problems cannot be solved at all.

How it reads

Each chapter is a complete story, and the series has almost no continuing plot. The mood is unhurried and melancholy, and the drawings of forest, river and weather do as much work as the dialogue. It sits close to iyashikei in tone while being more willing to end sadly.

Recognition

It won the general category of the Kodansha Manga Award in 2003 and an Excellence Prize at the Japan Media Arts Festival the same year. Its anime adaptation is widely considered one of the most faithful ever made.

How to read it

There is no story arc to follow. Each chapter introduces one mushi and the person it has touched: a child whose ears hear sounds from nowhere, a village where rain never stops, a boy whose drawings come to life, a woman who sleeps through winter. Small details of Ginko's past emerge across the series, most fully in a chapter about how he lost his eye and his memory.

Adaptations

Artland's anime ran in 2005–2006, and a second series, Mushishi: Next Passage, followed in 2014, with two specials, adapting almost every chapter. Katsuhiro Ōtomo directed a live-action film in 2006.

Reading it today

Complete in ten volumes. It is best read slowly, one chapter at a time. Our guide to slice of life and iyashikei places it beside the quiet stories it resembles.

title: The Rose of Versailles
synopsis: A woman raised as a man commands Marie Antoinette's guard in the years before the French Revolution, in one of the most influential shojo manga ever drawn. Filed under 8, the ledger.
body:
8Title sums to 89 and reduces to 8 — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

What it is

Riyoko Ikeda's The Rose of Versailles ran in Shueisha's Margaret from 1972 to 1973 and was collected in ten volumes. It follows Marie Antoinette from her arrival in France to the guillotine, and alongside her Oscar François de Jarjayes, the daughter of a noble family raised as a son to inherit her father's military post, who becomes commander of the queen's guard.

How it works

The series began as Marie Antoinette's story, but readers took to Oscar, and she became its centre. Her arc, from loyal servant of the crown to someone who sides with the people of Paris, carries the political story of the Revolution, while her relationship with André, her servant and companion since childhood, carries the romance.

Why it matters

It proved that shojo manga could take on history, politics and tragedy at length, and that a magazine for girls could sustain an epic. Its success opened space for the ambitious shojo of the 1970s.

Its life on stage

The Takarazuka Revue, an all-female theatre company, adapted it in 1974, and the production became one of the company's defining shows, revived many times since. A 1979 anime adaptation took the story further abroad, especially in France and Italy, where it remains well known.

How the story is divided

The first part is Marie Antoinette's arrival as a girl, her life at Louis XV's court and her rivalry with Madame du Barry. The middle follows the queen's love for the Swedish count Fersen, Oscar's own hopeless feelings for him, and the affair of the diamond necklace that ruins the queen's reputation. The last part is the Revolution: Oscar's turn to the people of Paris, the storming of the Bastille, and the queen's last years and death.

Adaptations and sequels

TMS Entertainment's anime (1979–1980) ran for 40 episodes and was directed in its second half by Osamu Dezaki. Jacques Demy's live-action film Lady Oscar appeared in 1979, and MAPPA's animated film opened in January 2025. Ikeda added side stories in 1984 and 1985, and new episodes from 2013 to 2018. It has sold more than 23 million copies.

Reading it today

Complete in ten volumes. Our entry on Riyoko Ikeda covers her later work.

title: The Poe Clan
synopsis: Two boys who will never grow older drift through two centuries of European history as members of a clan of vampires. The title reduces to 9 — the closing.
body:
9Filed under 9. The Closing takes a completion, and this entry is hands on one.

What it is

Moto Hagio's The Poe Clan appeared in Shogakukan's Bessatsu Shōjo Comic from 1972 to 1976. Edgar, made a vampire as a boy in the eighteenth century, brings his friend Allan into the clan, and the two wander through Europe across the following two centuries, unable to age, settle or be known.

How it is told

The series is not told in order. Its episodes jump between decades, and the same events are seen from different characters' points of view, so that the reader assembles Edgar's history in fragments. The structure suits a story about time passing around characters who cannot change.

What it is about

The vampirism is less about horror than about loss: of family, of an ordinary life, of every human attachment Edgar forms. The story's melancholy, its beautiful boys and its intense friendships set a tone that shojo manga would return to for decades.

Why it matters

Together with They Were Eleven, it won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 1976, and it is one of the founding works of the generation of women creators known as the Year 24 Group. Hagio returned to the series in 2016, more than forty years after it ended, to wide attention in Japan.

How it is organised

The original stories range from 1754, when Edgar and his sister Marybelle are taken into the clan, to the 1970s. The best known include the story of how Allan joins Edgar in nineteenth-century England, and stories told by people who glimpse the two boys, unchanged, across the centuries.

The sequels

Hagio returned to the world in 2016 with Haru no Yume, followed by Unicorn (2018–2019), The Secret Garden (2019–2021) and Blue Pandora, which began in 2022, all in Flowers. The Takarazuka Revue staged a musical adaptation in 2018 and revived it in 2021.

Reading it today

Read the original first. Our guide to the Year 24 Group places it among the works that changed shōjo manga.

title: GeGeGe no Kitarō
synopsis: A one-eyed yokai boy born in a graveyard protects humans from the more dangerous spirits of Japanese folklore. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4A 4 by its title: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

What it is

Shigeru Mizuki's Kitarō stories began in the rental-book market in 1960 as Hakaba Kitarō, "Graveyard Kitarō", reworking a character from prewar kamishibai street theatre. They moved to Weekly Shōnen Magazine in 1965 and were renamed GeGeGe no Kitarō in 1967, shortly before the first anime adaptation.

The cast

Kitarō is the last survivor of a ghost tribe, born in a grave after his mother's death. He is accompanied by his father, reduced to a talking eyeball who rides on his head or bathes in a teacup, the scheming half-yokai Nezumi-otoko and the cat girl Neko-musume. Most stories pit them against yokai who prey on people.

The folklore

Mizuki drew on the Edo-period catalogues of yokai and on stories he heard as a child, and his designs became, for many Japanese readers, the standard image of these creatures. Kitarō's stories are a guided tour of traditional folklore as much as adventures.

Why it matters

Kitarō has been adapted for television in every decade since the 1960s, and he is one of the most familiar characters in Japan. The series is largely responsible for the yokai boom that runs through manga and anime, from Mushishi to contemporary supernatural action.

How it is organised

Most stories are a few chapters long: a yokai causes trouble, Kitarō is called in, and he defeats or outwits it, often with the help of Nezumi-otoko, whose loyalty depends on what he can earn. Some stories are long wars, against Western monsters such as Dracula or against great Japanese yokai like Nurarihyon. Mizuki returned to the character for decades in different magazines, so the series has many versions.

Adaptations

Television anime were made in 1968, 1971, 1985, 1996, 2007 and 2018. The film The Birth of Kitarō: The Mystery of GeGeGe (2023), about Kitarō's father, became a hit, and live-action films appeared in 2007 and 2008.

Reading it today

Drawn & Quarterly's English selection is the easiest way in. Our entry on Shigeru Mizuki covers his war manga and history of Japan, and our glossary entry on yokai explains the folklore.

title: Maison Ikkoku
synopsis: A struggling student falls for the young widowed manager of his run-down boarding house, in a slow, funny romance that grows up with its characters. Filed under 5, the turn.
body:
5The letters of this title total 50, a 5 — the number of freedom, disruption, and restless movement.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Maison Ikkoku ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1980 to 1987 and was collected in 15 volumes. Yusaku Godai, a student failing his entrance exams, lives in a shabby boarding house full of nosy, hard-drinking neighbours. When Kyoko Otonashi arrives as its new manager, he falls in love with her, not knowing at first that she is a widow.

How it works

The comedy is in the house: neighbours who invade Godai's room through a hole in the wall, misunderstandings, rivals, a ridiculous tennis coach. The drama is in Kyoko's grief for her husband and Godai's slow progress from hopeless student to an adult she could choose.

Time passes

Unlike many romantic comedies, Maison Ikkoku lets its characters age. Godai graduates, struggles to find work and changes, and the story follows the years it takes, which gives its ending real weight.

Why it matters

It is often cited as one of the best romance manga ever made and as the work that showed Takahashi's range beyond broad comedy. It is a strong recommendation for readers who think manga romance means only school stories.

How the story is divided

The story follows about seven years. The early volumes are Godai's failed exams, his arrival at university and his first attempts to be noticed by Kyoko, against the competition of the handsome tennis coach Mitaka. The middle volumes follow Godai's graduation into a world without jobs, his work at a nursery school and the arrival of new rivals on both sides. The last volumes are about whether Kyoko can let go of her husband, and a proposal that has to wait for its answer.

Adaptations

Studio Deen's anime ran for 96 episodes from 1986 to 1988 and adapted the whole story, followed by a film. Live-action versions appeared in 1986 and 2007.

title: Ranma ½
synopsis: A martial artist cursed to turn into a girl when splashed with cold water is engaged against his will, in a fast, chaotic action comedy. Read from the pairing, as a 2.
body:
2Two — cooperation. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Ranma ½ ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1987 to 1996 and was collected in 38 volumes. Ranma Saotome fell into a cursed spring in China while training, and now turns into a girl when splashed with cold water and back with hot. His father, who turns into a panda, has promised him in marriage to Akane Tendo, a martial artist who wants nothing to do with him.

How it works

The curse is a machine for comedy. A rival who turns into a pig, a Chinese warrior who becomes a cat, a growing crowd of fiancées and challengers, and a new martial-arts "school" for every absurd activity, from tea ceremony to figure skating, keep the series in constant motion.

The fights

Beneath the farce, Ranma ½ is a well-made martial arts manga, with techniques that have rules and fights that turn on cleverness. Takahashi mixes slapstick and choreography in a way many later action comedies imitated.

Why it matters

Its anime adaptation was one of the first to find a wide audience in North America in the 1990s, and the series became a gateway to manga for many Western readers. Its play with gender, light as it often is, gave it a lasting place in discussions of the medium.

How the story is divided

There are few long arcs: most stories are a few chapters long and introduce a new rival, fiancée or school of martial arts. The cast grows from the Tendō household to include Ryōga, who gets lost everywhere and turns into a pig; Shampoo, an Amazon from China who turns into a cat; Ukyō, Ranma's childhood friend and okonomiyaki chef; and the Kunō siblings. The final volumes return to China and Jusenkyō, the cursed springs, for the series' biggest battle and a wedding that ends exactly as readers might expect.

Adaptations

Studio Deen's anime ran for 161 episodes from 1989 to 1992. MAPPA's remake began on Nippon Television and Netflix in 2024, with a second season in 2025 and a third in October 2026. A live-action television special aired in 2011. The manga has passed 55 million copies.

Reading it today

Complete in 38 volumes. It can be read in short bursts, and the remake follows the manga more closely than the first anime.

title: Inuyasha
synopsis: A modern schoolgirl falls through a well into feudal Japan and joins a half-demon to recover the shattered fragments of a sacred jewel. 35 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Reduced, this title gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Inuyasha ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1996 to 2008 and was collected in 56 volumes. Kagome Higurashi falls through the well at her family's shrine into Japan's Sengoku period, where she frees the half-demon Inuyasha and accidentally shatters the Shikon Jewel, which grants great power to whoever holds it.

How it works

The quest to gather the jewel's shards gives the series an open structure: a new village, a new yokai, a new shard. A small band forms around Inuyasha and Kagome, each with a reason to hunt the villain Naraku, and the story gradually reveals the tragedy that bound Inuyasha to the priestess Kikyo fifty years before.

The mix

It combines adventure, horror, romance and comedy. Takahashi's yokai are drawn from folklore but given her own designs, and the love triangle across two lives became one of the most argued-over in manga fandom.

Why it matters

It was one of the most popular manga and anime of the turn of the century, internationally as well as in Japan, and it is an early and influential example of a story that sends a modern character into a historical or fantastic world.

How the story is divided

The early volumes gather the band: Kagome and Inuyasha, then the young fox demon Shippō, the lecherous monk Miroku and the demon slayer Sango, each wronged by Naraku. The middle of the series is a long pursuit across Japan, with the revived Kikyō, Inuyasha's elder half-brother Sesshōmaru and the wolf demon Kōga crossing their path. The last volumes return to the Shikon Jewel itself and the question of what Kagome will choose when the quest ends.

Adaptations

Sunrise's anime ran for 167 episodes from 2000 to 2004 and stopped before the end of the story. Inuyasha: The Final Act (2009–2010) adapted the remaining volumes, and a sequel series, Yashahime: Princess Half-Demon (2020–2022), followed the next generation. Four films were also produced.

Reading it today

Complete in 56 volumes, it is long but easy to read, and the arc structure means each few volumes feel complete. Readers who stopped with the first anime can pick up the story in The Final Act or in the manga where the anime left off.

title: Chihayafuru
synopsis: A girl discovers competitive karuta, a fast card game built on a classical poetry anthology, and sets out to become the best player in Japan. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4A 4 by its title: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

What it is

Yuki Suetsugu's Chihayafuru ran in Kodansha's Be Love from 2007 to 2022 and was collected in 50 volumes. Chihaya Ayase learns competitive karuta from a transfer student as a child, loses touch with him and their friend, and rebuilds the game in high school with a new club and a goal: to become Queen, the top women's title.

The game

Competitive karuta uses the cards of the Hyakunin Isshu, a thirteenth-century anthology of a hundred poems. A reader recites the first part of a poem; players race to strike the card bearing its ending. It demands memory, hearing and physical speed, and Suetsugu makes it as intense as any sport.

The poems

The series takes its title from a poem by Ariwara no Narihira, and poems from the anthology run through the story, each explained in context. Readers come away knowing classical verse they might never have met at school.

Recognition

It won the Manga Taishō in 2009 and was adapted as an anime and as a series of live-action films. It is widely credited with a surge of interest in competitive karuta in Japan.

How the story is divided

The first volumes tell the story of Chihaya, Arata and Taichi as children, and how they lost each other. The high-school part follows the founding of the Mizusawa karuta club, team tournaments and Chihaya's rise through the individual ranks. The last third builds to the Queen and Master matches, the two national title matches, and to a romantic choice that is also about how each of them plays the game.

Adaptations

Madhouse's anime ran for three seasons (2011, 2013 and 2019–2020). Three live-action films followed in 2016 and 2018, and a drama, Chihayafuru: Meguri, set ten years later, aired in 2025. Suetsugu continues the story in a sequel manga, Chihayafuru plus Kimi ga Tame, which began in 2023. The original series has passed 29 million copies and won the Kodansha Manga Award for shōjo manga as well as the Manga Taishō.

Complete in 50 volumes. The anime stops well before the end, so readers who have watched it should continue in the manga.

title: Hikaru no Go
synopsis: A sixth-grader is possessed by the ghost of a Heian-era go master, and the game neither of them can let go of becomes his life. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11An 11 by its title: visionary (master 11), and therefore the signal.

What it is

Hikaru no Go, written by Yumi Hotta and drawn by Takeshi Obata, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1998 to 2003 and was collected in 23 volumes. Hikaru Shindo finds an old go board in his grandfather's attic and is haunted by Fujiwara-no-Sai, a go instructor at the Heian court who longs to play the "divine move".

How it works

At first Hikaru plays only as Sai's hands. As he grows interested in the game himself, and in his rival Akira Toya, the son of the strongest player in Japan, he begins to play on his own, and the story becomes one about the gap between the two of them and what Sai will do when Hikaru no longer needs him.

Go on the page

The games were supervised by a professional player, and the boards shown are real positions. The series makes the game dramatic without asking the reader to understand it, through the players' faces, the timing of stones and commentary from onlookers.

Why it matters

It set off a go boom among children in Japan and beyond, and it is the model for a whole category of manga about board games and quiet competition. It is also the first of Obata's major collaborations, followed by Death Note and Bakuman.

How the story is divided

The first part is Hikaru's discovery of go through Sai, his first games against Akira and his time in his school's go club. The second follows him as an insei, a trainee for professional status, through the professional exam. The third is his early professional career, which turns on a turning point in his partnership with Sai that readers still talk about. The last volumes follow Hikaru as a young professional, ending with a youth tournament against China and Korea.

Adaptations

Pierrot's anime ran for 75 episodes from 2001 to 2003, followed by a New Year's special. It won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 2000 and the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize New Creator Prize in 2003.

title: Bakuman
synopsis: Two high-school boys set out to become manga creators in Weekly Shonen Jump, in a series about the magazine, written for it. Read from the closing, as a 9.
body:
9A 9 by its title: humanitarian & sage, and therefore the closing.

What it is

Bakuman, by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata, the team behind Death Note, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2008 to 2012 and was collected in 20 volumes. Moritaka Mashiro, an artist, and Akito Takagi, a writer, team up as teenagers with a goal: a hit series in Jump and an anime adaptation, in which Mashiro's love, an aspiring voice actress, will play the heroine.

How it works

It is a sports manga in which the sport is making manga. The tournaments are the reader surveys, the rivals are other young creators, and the coaches are editors. Each stage of the process, from the storyboard and one-shot to serialisation, cancellation and the fight for placement in the magazine, is turned into drama.

How much is true?

A great deal of the process is accurate, and the series is one of the most detailed public accounts of how Jump works. It is also a story Jump chose to publish about itself, and it treats the magazine's punishing system as a challenge to rise to more than a problem.

Why it matters

For readers curious about the industry, Bakuman is the most entertaining introduction there is. Mashiro's uncle, a creator who died after years of overwork, gives the story an undertone that the cheerful surface never quite removes.

How the story is divided

The first volumes are Mashiro and Takagi's apprenticeship: their first one-shots, their editor Hattori, and the arrival of Eiji Niizuma, a teenage genius who becomes their rival and model. Their first serial, Detective Trap, is cancelled; a gag series, Tanto, follows, and so do the internal battles over reader surveys. The second half follows Perfect Crime Party, their first real hit, and their last series, Reversi, written to beat Niizuma in the rankings and earn the anime that will fulfil Mashiro's promise.

Adaptations

J.C.Staff's anime ran for three seasons from 2010 to 2013 and adapted the whole manga. A live-action film followed in 2015.

Reading it today
