title: The Promised Neverland
synopsis: Children at an idyllic orphanage discover that they are being raised as food, and plan an escape. Read from the pairing, as a 2.
body:
2Two — cooperation. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

The Promised Neverland, written by Kaiu Shirai and drawn by Posuka Demizu, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2016 to 2020 and was collected in 20 volumes. Grace Field House is a happy orphanage where children are cared for by a loving woman they call Mom, play in the woods and take daily tests. When one of them is sent away to be adopted, Emma and Norman, the brightest children, follow her to the gate and discover the truth: the orphanage is a farm, and its children are raised to be eaten by demons.

How it works

The first arc is a psychological thriller. Emma, Norman and Ray, the three oldest and cleverest children, plan an escape under the eyes of Mom, Isabella, who is as clever as they are and knows that they know. Every conversation is a test of trust and deception. Later arcs follow the children into the world beyond the wall.

The craft

Demizu's art, with its storybook detail, makes the house feel warm, and so makes the horror worse. Shirai builds the plot like a strategy game, and the children's refusal to abandon anyone, including the youngest, is what makes their plans so hard.

Why it matters

It brought a horror thriller to the heart of Jump and was a major international success. Its 2019 anime's first season was widely praised, while its second season, which departed sharply from the manga, was strongly criticised by fans.

How the story is divided

The first arc, about five volumes, is the escape from Grace Field House, the orphanage where Emma, Norman and Ray discover what they are being raised for. It is a tight psychological thriller, and the part of the series readers praise most. The rest follows the children into the outside world: hiding, searching for allies, a brutal hunting ground called Goldy Pond, and the effort to change the system rather than only escape it.

Adaptations

CloverWorks' first anime season (2019) was widely acclaimed. The second (2021) skipped major arcs, including Goldy Pond, and compressed and changed the ending, and was heavily criticised. A Japanese live-action film was released in 2020.

Reading it today

title: Assassination Classroom
synopsis: A smiling, octopus-like creature that has destroyed most of the Moon becomes a class's teacher, and gives them a year to kill him before he destroys the Earth. Filed under 5, the turn.
body:
5The letters of this title total 77, a 5 — the number of freedom, disruption, and restless movement.

What it is

Yūsei Matsui's Assassination Classroom ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2012 to 2016 and was collected in 21 volumes. A yellow, tentacled creature that can move at twenty times the speed of sound has destroyed seventy per cent of the Moon. He announces that he will destroy the Earth next March, but first he wants to teach Class 3-E, the school's class of failures, at an elite junior high. The government offers the students a huge reward if they can kill him. They name him Koro-sensei.

How it works

The students plot and practise assassination attempts, with weapons supplied by the government that harm only him, and he dodges every one, while giving them the best education they have ever had. He teaches academic subjects, but also confidence, strategy and how to find their own strengths. Each student gets a chapter in which they find a talent.

The heart

The premise is a joke, but the story is about what a good teacher does. As the year passes, the students learn the truth about Koro-sensei's past, and the question becomes whether they can do what they were asked to do.

Why it matters

It was a major Jump hit, adapted as an anime and two live-action films, and is often recommended for its mix of comedy, action and emotional payoff. Many readers name its ending as one of the most moving in shōnen manga.

How the story is divided

The first part introduces Class 3-E, its human teachers, Karasuma and the assassin Irina, and the students' first attempts. The middle of the series includes a trip to an island where the class is attacked, a midterm war with the elite Class A and its leader Gakushū Asano, and the arrival of Itona, a student with tentacles of his own. The last part reveals Koro-sensei's past as the assassin known as the Reaper, and the class's final choice.

Adaptations

Lerche's anime ran for two seasons (2015 and 2016) and adapted the whole manga. Two live-action films followed in 2015 and 2016.

Complete in 21 volumes. Our entry on Yūsei Matsui covers his other works.

title: Blue Period
synopsis: A popular, bored high-school student discovers painting, and sets out to get into Japan's most competitive art university. 53 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8The letters of this title total 53, an 8 — the number of money, authority, and the machinery of ambition.

What it is

Tsubasa Yamaguchi's Blue Period has run in Kodansha's Monthly Afternoon since 2017. Yatora Yaguchi is a high-school student who is good at everything: he gets top grades, stays out drinking with his friends and is liked by everyone. Yet he feels empty. When he sees a painting by an older student in the art room, and then tries to paint the blue light of Shibuya at dawn, he feels for the first time that he has communicated something real.

How it works

Yatora decides to apply to Tokyo University of the Arts, the most competitive art school in Japan, which accepts only a tiny fraction of applicants. The series follows his training: drawing exercises, composition, colour, critique and the brutal entrance exams. Real techniques and ways of thinking about art are explained in detail, and readers learn alongside him.

The characters

Yatora's classmates and rivals are drawn with care, especially Ryūji Ayukawa, who prefers to be called Yuka, and whose struggles with family and identity run alongside Yatora's. The series is honest about self-doubt and how hard it is to know whether you are good enough.

Why it matters

It won the Manga Taishō in 2020 and was adapted as an anime in 2021 and a live-action film in 2024. Its account of entrance-exam training is specific enough to work as a guide, and it has drawn many readers to drawing and painting.

How the story is divided

The first part is Yatora's discovery of painting, his time in the art club and at a preparatory art school, and his two-stage entrance exam for Tokyo University of the Arts. The second part follows him at the university, where his technique counts for less than he expected and he must decide what kind of artist he wants to be, with exhibitions, part-time teaching and new friends and rivals.

Adaptations

Seven Arcs' anime (2021) covers the entrance exams. A stage play followed in 2022 and a live-action film in 2024. The manga won the Kodansha Manga Award and the Manga Taishō in 2020.

Reading it today

Still running, with 19 volumes by 2026. The anime ends with the exams, so readers who know it can begin with the university years.

title: Kaiju No. 8
synopsis: A 32-year-old who cleans up dead monsters for a living suddenly turns into one, just as he gets his last chance to join the force that fights them. Read from the closing, as a 9.
body:
9A 9 by its title: humanitarian & sage, and therefore the closing.

What it is

Naoya Matsumoto's Kaiju No. 8 ran on Shueisha's Shōnen Jump+ from 2020 to 2025. In a Japan regularly attacked by giant monsters, kaiju, the Defense Force fights them, and private companies clean up the bodies. Kafka Hibino, aged 32, works for one of those companies. As a boy he promised his friend Mina Ashiro that they would fight kaiju together. She became a famous captain; he failed the entrance exam and gave up.

How it works

A small creature enters Kafka's body, and he becomes able to transform into a powerful kaiju himself. The Defense Force names him Kaiju No. 8 and hunts him. At the same time, the age limit for recruits is raised, and he applies again. He must train and fight as a human while hiding that he is the monster they are looking for.

The hero

Kafka is unusual for a shōnen hero: an adult who had given up on his dream, and who is mocked for being too old. His story is about a second chance, and his relationship with the young recruits, especially the ambitious Reno Ichikawa, shows an older man encouraging the next generation.

Why it matters

It became one of the biggest hits of Jump+ and a major example of web serialisation reaching a mass audience. Its 2024 anime by Production I.G was widely watched around the world, and it draws on the long Japanese tradition of kaiju films and tokusatsu.

How the story is divided

Kafka Hibino, a 32-year-old who cleans up after monster attacks, gains the power to turn into a kaiju himself, and joins the defence force he once failed to get into. The story follows his time in the force, the discovery of his secret, his fight to prove he is on humanity's side, and an escalating war against an intelligent kaiju who commands others.

Adaptations

The series ran on the Shōnen Jump+ app, where it set readership records. Production I.G's anime began in 2024, with a second season in 2025.

Reading it today

Complete in 16 volumes, it is a short, fast read, and its older hero is rare in battle manga. The glossary entry on kaiju traces the monster tradition it draws on.

title: Barefoot Gen
synopsis: A boy in Hiroshima survives the atomic bomb that kills most of his family, and struggles to live in the ruined city that follows. Read from the closing, as a 9.
body:
9Nine — reckoning. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Keiji Nakazawa's Barefoot Gen began in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1973 and, after it left Jump, continued in a series of smaller magazines until 1987. It was collected in 10 volumes. Gen Nakaoka is a boy in Hiroshima during the Second World War. His father, an artist, openly opposes the war, and the family is persecuted by neighbours and police as traitors. On 6 August 1945 the atomic bomb falls.

How it works

Gen's father, sister and younger brother are trapped under their burning house, and Gen and his pregnant mother cannot save them. The first volumes show the bombing and its immediate aftermath in unflinching detail: burned bodies, radiation sickness, starvation and the collapse of the city. Later volumes follow Gen through the occupation years, as he fights to survive, cares for orphans and grows up.

From life

The story is closely based on Nakazawa's own experience. He was six when the bomb fell, and lost his father, sister and brother in the same way. He had already told the story directly in a short autobiographical work, I Saw It (1972), before turning it into a long-form series.

Why it matters

It is one of the most important works of war testimony in any medium, and has been read by generations of Japanese schoolchildren. Volunteer translators carried it into English and many other languages, and its anime films (1983, 1986) brought it to more viewers. Its graphic violence and its criticism of the wartime emperor system have also made it the subject of repeated arguments over whether it belongs in school libraries.

title: Lone Wolf and Cub
synopsis: The shogun's executioner, framed and disgraced, wanders Edo-period Japan as an assassin for hire, pushing his infant son in a weaponised baby cart. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3The letters of this title total 57, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

What it is

Lone Wolf and Cub, written by Kazuo Koike and drawn by Goseki Kojima, ran in Futabasha's Weekly Manga Action from 1970 to 1976 and was collected in 28 volumes. Ogami Ittō was the shogun's official executioner until the scheming Yagyū clan murdered his wife and framed him for treason. Refusing to die, he takes his infant son Daigorō on the road to seek revenge, earning money as an assassin.

How it works

Most stories are self-contained episodes in which a client hires Ittō for a killing, which usually reveals something about the samurai code, the cruelty of the period or the lives of ordinary people. Daigorō rides in a wooden baby cart concealing blades and guns. Over the whole series runs the war between Ittō and the Yagyū, building to a final confrontation.

The art

Kojima's brushwork is restrained and cinematic, with long, nearly silent sequences of landscape, walking and sudden violence. Koike's scripts are full of historical detail about Edo-period customs, law and swordsmanship, and they give Daigorō's silent watching as much weight as his father's battles.

Why it matters

It is a masterpiece of gekiga and of samurai fiction. It was adapted into six films in the 1970s, which were later cut together abroad as Shogun Assassin, and its English edition in the 1980s, with covers by Frank Miller, introduced many American comics readers to manga. Its influence can be seen in later Western stories of a killer travelling with a child.

title: Glass Mask
synopsis: A poor, ordinary-looking girl with a genius for acting competes with a privileged rival for the right to play a legendary role. Read from the telling, as a 3.
body:
3A 3 by its title: creative communicator, and therefore the telling.

What it is

Suzue Miuchi's Glass Mask began in Hakusensha's Hana to Yume in 1976 and has been collected in 49 volumes, with its ending still unpublished. Maya Kitajima is a poor girl with no looks, no money and no talent anyone can see, except an extraordinary ability to become any role she plays. She is discovered by Chigusa Tsukikage, a once-great actress, who owns the rights to a legendary play, The Crimson Goddess.

How it works

Maya's rival is Ayumi Himekawa, the beautiful, gifted daughter of a famous actress and director, who has worked for everything she has. The two compete through stage plays, films and television towards the right to play the Crimson Goddess. Each arc is built around a performance, and Maya's process of finding a character is described in detail.

The romance

Maya is supported by an anonymous fan who sends her purple roses. He is secretly Masumi Hayami, the cold head of a talent agency who seems to be her enemy. The slow, painful romance between them is one of the most famous in shōjo manga.

Why it matters

It is one of the best-selling shōjo manga ever and a classic of the genre's grand melodrama. It has been adapted as anime, television drama and stage plays, and its intense rivalry and dedication to art remain models for later stories about performers.

How the story is divided

Each arc is a production. Maya's early roles, among them Beth in Little Women, establish her gift; she and Ayumi both play Helen Keller in rival productions of The Miracle Worker; Maya becomes a television star, is ruined by a scandal and works her way back from street theatre; and she plays a wolf girl raised in the wild. The long final arc is the competition between Maya and Ayumi for The Crimson Goddess, rehearsed in the mountains under Tsukikage, while Maya and Masumi move towards the truth about the purple roses.

Adaptations

Anime were made in 1984 and 2005, a television drama in 1997 and 1998, and many stage versions, including a production of The Crimson Goddess itself.

Reading it today

The story has been on hiatus since the 49th volume in 2012. Readers should start knowing it may never be finished. Our glossary entry on shōjo explains the tradition it belongs to.

title: Candy Candy
altTitles: キャンディ・キャンディ
synopsis: A cheerful orphan in early twentieth-century America meets love, loss and hardship, and never stops smiling. The title reduces to 4 — the structure.
body:
4A 4 by its title: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

What it is

Candy Candy, written by Kyōko Mizuki and drawn by Yumiko Igarashi, ran in Kodansha's Nakayoshi from 1975 to 1979 and was collected in 9 volumes. Candice White is a freckled, tomboyish orphan raised at the Pony's Home in the American Midwest in the early twentieth century. Taken in as a companion by the wealthy, cruel Leagan family, she meets the people who will shape her life.

How it works

The story follows Candy from childhood through an English boarding school to training as a nurse during the First World War. It is full of melodrama: the death of her first love, Anthony, a doomed romance with the rebellious Terry, and the mystery of her protector, the Prince of the Hill. Through every disaster Candy remains brave and kind.

The style

Igarashi's art is the classic 1970s shōjo look: huge sparkling eyes, flowing hair, flowers and elaborate period costume. Mizuki's story draws on Western children's literature, from Anne of Green Gables to Daddy-Long-Legs.

Why it matters

It was a huge hit, and its 1976 anime spread it across Europe, Latin America and Asia. A long legal dispute between its two creators over the rights, settled by Japan's Supreme Court in 2001 in Mizuki's favour as co-author, has kept the manga out of print for years.

How the story is divided

The first part is Candy's childhood: the Pony's Home, the Leagans' cruelty, and her meetings with the Andrew family's boys, Anthony, Archie and Stear, and with the Prince of the Hill. After Anthony's death, Candy is adopted by the mysterious head of the Andrew family and sent to school in London, where she meets Terry. The last part follows her return to America, her nursing training, the war and the loss of Stear, her parting from Terry, and the revelation of who her protector has been.

Adaptations

Toei's anime ran for 115 episodes from 1976 to 1979.

Reading it today

Because of the rights dispute, new editions of the manga have not been published for many years, and most readers know it through the anime. Mizuki published a novel, Candy Candy Final Story, in 2010.

title: Crayon Shin-chan
synopsis: A rude, shameless five-year-old in the Tokyo suburbs torments his parents, his friends and everyone else, and is somehow lovable. Filed under 8, the ledger.
body:
8Title sums to 71 and reduces to 8 — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

What it is

Yoshito Usui's Crayon Shin-chan began in Futabasha's Weekly Manga Action in 1990 and later moved to Manga Town, running until 2010 and filling 50 volumes. Shinnosuke Nohara, known as Shin-chan, is a five-year-old in Kasukabe, a commuter town in Saitama Prefecture. He flirts with grown women, does a rude dance with his bottom, says exactly what he thinks and drives his parents, Misae and Hiroshi, to despair.

How it works

The strips and short chapters are mostly gags about family life, kindergarten and the neighbourhood. Shin-chan's mother struggles with housework and money, his father with his job and his feet, and the comedy comes from a child's misunderstandings of adult life. It was published in a magazine for adults, and many of the jokes are for them.

A family story

Under the crudeness, the Noharas are a loving, ordinary middle-class family, and the series, especially its films, often turns to warm stories about parents and children.

Why it matters

Its anime, running since 1992, made Shin-chan one of Japan's most famous characters, and its annual films are hugely popular. Usui died in an accident while hiking in 2009, and his assistants continued the series as New Crayon Shin-chan from 2010.

How it is organised

The series has no plot. It grows by adding characters: Shin-chan's baby sister, Himawari, born partway through; his friends at Futaba kindergarten, among them Kazama, Nene, Masao and Bo-chan; his teachers; and the dog Shiro. Some chapters are longer stories, and the characters age only slowly, so the family has been five years old, and thirty-five, for more than three decades.

Adaptations

Shin-Ei Animation's anime has run on TV Asahi since 1992, and a new film has been released almost every year since 1993. Several, among them The Adult Empire Strikes Back (2001) and The Battle of the Warring States (2002), are counted among the best Japanese animated films of their years.

title: Chibi Maruko-chan
synopsis: A lazy, daydreaming girl in 1970s Shizuoka lives an ordinary childhood with her family and classmates, based on the author's own. 73 in the letters, reducing to 1.
body:
1Title sums to 73 and reduces to 1 — The Opening, where the reference files a first move.

What it is

Momoko Sakura's Chibi Maruko-chan began in Shueisha's girls' magazine Ribon in 1986 and ran there regularly until 1996, with occasional chapters afterwards. Momoko Sakura, nicknamed Maruko, is a third-grader in the town of Shimizu, in Shizuoka Prefecture, in the 1970s. She is lazy, greedy and fond of daydreaming, and lives with her parents, her older sister and her grandparents.

How it works

Each chapter is a small episode of childhood: a school trip, a festival, a craze for a pop idol, an argument with her sister, a scheme to avoid homework. The characters are her real family and classmates, gently exaggerated. A narrator comments on Maruko's behaviour with dry, adult humour.

Nostalgia

The series is set a decade or more before it was written, and recreates the details of 1970s childhood: television shows, snacks, toys and the rhythms of family life. Readers who grew up then found their own memories in it, and younger readers found an ordinary past.

Why it matters

Its anime, broadcast from 1990, became a national hit, and its theme song was a best-seller. It remains on television, and Maruko is one of the most familiar characters in Japan. Sakura, who also wrote best-selling essays, died in 2018.

How it is organised

Each chapter is complete, and the year passes through its seasons, from New Year to summer holidays. The cast grows around Maruko: her grandfather Tomozō, who adores her; her sharp older sister; her school friends, among them the quiet Tamae and the class's eccentric boys; and her teacher. Sakura based the stories on her own childhood in Shimizu, which has made the town a place of pilgrimage.

Adaptations

Nippon Animation's anime ran from 1990 to 1992 and again from 1995, and is still broadcast weekly. Its theme, "Odoru Pompokolin", was one of the best-selling singles of 1990. There have also been films and live-action dramas.

title: Saint Young Men
synopsis: Jesus and the Buddha take a holiday on Earth, sharing a cheap flat in the Tokyo suburbs and trying to live like ordinary young men. The title reduces to 6 — the care.
body:
6Filed under 6. The Care takes an obligation, and this entry is protects one.

What it is

Hikaru Nakamura's Saint Young Men has run in Kodansha's Morning magazines since 2006. Jesus and the Buddha, after centuries of hard work, take a holiday on Earth. They rent a small apartment together in Tachikawa, a suburb of Tokyo, and live on a tight budget, shopping, going to the bathhouse, blogging and trying not to be recognised.

How it works

The comedy comes from two of the most important figures in human history dealing with ordinary modern life. Jesus loves shopping and blogs; the Buddha is careful with money and draws manga. Their miracles happen by accident: Jesus turns bathwater into wine when he relaxes, and animals gather around the Buddha. Many jokes depend on details from the Bible and the Buddhist scriptures.

The tone

The series is affectionate rather than mocking. Jesus and the Buddha are kind, good friends and very funny, and it pokes fun at modern Japanese life more than at religion. Other figures, including saints, archangels and Buddhist deities, visit them.

Why it matters

It became a best-seller and was adapted as an anime film (2013) and live-action productions. It is a much-loved example of gentle comedy built on an outrageous premise, and Nakamura's other major work, Arakawa Under the Bridge, shares its warm absurdity.

How it is organised

There is no plot: each chapter is a day in the two saints' life in Tachikawa, a festival, a trip to the sea, a visit to a theme park, a part-time job. Visitors from heaven and the Buddhist paradise appear regularly, among them Peter and Andrew, who come to check on Jesus, the archangels, and the Buddha's disciples, as do the neighbours and children who have no idea who their tenants really are.

Adaptations

An animated film (2013) and short episodes were followed by live-action adaptations directed by Yūichi Fukuda.

Reading it today

Any volume can be read alone. The jokes need some familiarity with the Bible and with Buddhism, though not much. Our entry on Hikaru Nakamura covers her other work.

title: Thermae Romae
synopsis: An ancient Roman architect who designs public baths keeps slipping through time into modern Japan, and takes its bathing ideas home. The title reduces to 5 — the turn.
body:
5Five — change. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Mari Yamazaki's Thermae Romae ran in Enterbrain's Comic Beam from 2008 to 2013 and was collected in 6 volumes. Lucius Quintus Modestus is an architect in Rome in the time of the emperor Hadrian, who designs public baths and worries that his ideas are out of date. One day, while bathing, he is sucked down a drain and emerges in a public bathhouse in modern Japan.

How it works

Each episode follows the same pattern. Lucius is transported to Japan, sees an ordinary bathing invention, such as a bottled drink after a bath, a home bathtub or a hot spring resort, believes it is the work of a remarkable slave people he calls the "flat-faced tribe", and takes the idea back to Rome, where it makes him famous.

The comedy

The joke is the collision of two bath cultures, ancient Roman and modern Japanese, and of Lucius's serious amazement at things the reader takes for granted. Yamazaki, who studied in Italy, draws Roman history and architecture in detail, and the series is full of real information about both cultures.

Why it matters

It won the Manga Taishō and the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize Short Story Award in 2010. Its live-action films starring Hiroshi Abe (2012, 2014) were hits, and it is one of the best-known examples of time-slip comedy in manga.

How the story is divided

The first volumes are single episodes of Lucius's visits and inventions, which win him the favour of Hadrian. In the later volumes, Lucius is caught up in the politics of the empire's succession and travels to a Japanese hot-spring village, where he meets Satsuki, a young woman who studies Latin and who, in turn, finds her way to Rome. The series ends with Hadrian's death and Lucius's own fate.

Adaptations

Short anime episodes (2012) were followed by the live-action films starring Hiroshi Abe (2012 and 2014) and the Netflix anime Thermae Romae Novae (2022).

Reading it today

Complete in six volumes. Yamazaki's notes between chapters, on Roman and Japanese bathing, are part of the fun. Our guide to manga set in history outside Japan places it among its peers.

title: Kamui Den
synopsis: In Edo-period Japan, an outcast boy becomes a ninja, while peasants and a samurai struggle against a cruel feudal order. Read from the teaching, as a 33.
body:
33Thirty-three — service. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Sanpei Shirato's Kamui Den ran from 1964 to 1971 in Garo, a monthly magazine founded largely to publish it, with a second part following in the 1980s and 1990s. Set in the Edo period, it follows three young men from different classes: Kamui, born into the lowest caste of outcasts, who becomes a ninja to escape it; Shōsuke, a peasant who leads his village against oppression; and Ryūnosuke, a samurai whose family is destroyed by intrigue.

How it works

The story is an epic of the feudal system seen from below. It shows famine, taxation, uprisings, discrimination against outcasts and the violence of those in power, and it follows how the three men's lives cross. Much of it is about economics and class: how rice is grown, how it is taxed, and who suffers.

The politics

Shirato, the son of a left-wing painter, wrote Kamui Den as a Marxist history, and it was read eagerly by the student radicals of the 1960s. Its seriousness about history and society helped show that manga could be political literature.

Why it matters

It made Garo the home of alternative manga, which went on to publish artists such as Yoshiharu Tsuge, and it is one of the landmarks of gekiga. A separate, more action-centred story about Kamui, Kamui Gaiden, was adapted as an anime and as a live-action film.

How it is organised

The first part follows the three men's childhoods and youth in the same domain, as famine and the lord's policies drive the peasants towards revolt. Kamui escapes the outcast village by becoming a ninja, then deserts and is hunted by his own clan. Shōsuke organises the peasants and learns how the economy that crushes them works. Ryūnosuke, his family ruined, becomes a wandering swordsman. The second part, published from 1982, continues the story into wider politics.

Adaptations

The anime Ninpū Kamui Gaiden (1969) and Yōichi Sai's live-action film Kamui Gaiden (2009) adapted the separate spin-off about Kamui as a fugitive ninja.

Reading it today

No complete English translation exists. Our glossary entry on gekiga explains the movement it belongs to.

title: Kimagure Orange Road
altTitles: きまぐれオレンジ☆ロード
synopsis: A teenage boy from a family of secret psychics is caught between a cool, mysterious girl and her cheerful best friend. The title reduces to 3 — the telling.
body:
3A 3 by its title: creative communicator, and therefore the telling.

What it is

Izumi Matsumoto's Kimagure Orange Road ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1984 to 1987 and was collected in 18 volumes. Kyōsuke Kasuga is an indecisive high-school student whose family has psychic powers that they must keep hidden. After moving to a new town, he meets Madoka Ayukawa, a beautiful, cool girl with a reputation as a delinquent, and falls for her, only for her younger friend Hikaru to fall for him.

How it works

The series is a romantic comedy built on a love triangle. Kyōsuke cannot bring himself to hurt Hikaru or to tell Madoka how he feels, and his attempts to keep everyone happy make things worse. His family's powers, such as teleportation and moving objects, create comic emergencies and allow occasional fantasy episodes.

The mood

Matsumoto drew with soft, stylish art, and the series has a gentle, bittersweet atmosphere of summer, music and adolescence. Madoka, who plays the saxophone and hides her kindness behind a tough front, became one of the most iconic heroines of the 1980s.

Why it matters

It was one of the defining romantic comedies of 1980s shōnen manga, and its anime, from 1987, became a cult favourite abroad. It influenced many later love-triangle stories. Matsumoto's later career was limited by serious health problems.

How the story is divided

The first volumes set up the triangle: Kyōsuke's arrival, his first meetings with Madoka and Hikaru, and the summer that ties the three together. The middle volumes are comic episodes of school, part-time jobs at the café ABCB, and family powers going wrong, with Kyōsuke's sisters and cousin adding to the chaos. The last volumes bring Kyōsuke to the choice he has avoided for years, and end on the steps where he first met Madoka.

Adaptations

Pierrot's anime ran for 48 episodes from 1987 to 1988, followed by OVAs and the film I Want to Return to That Day (1988), which gave the triangle its own, sadder ending.

title: Blade of the Immortal
synopsis: A samurai cursed with immortality agrees to help a girl avenge her parents, as penance for the lives he has taken. Filed under 8, the ledger.
body:
8Title sums to 80 and reduces to 8 — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

What it is

Hiroaki Samura's Blade of the Immortal ran in Kodansha's Monthly Afternoon from 1993 to 2012 and was collected in 30 volumes. Manji is a rōnin who has killed a hundred men, among them his sister's husband. A mysterious old nun puts sacred bloodworms into his body, and now any wound he takes heals: severed limbs reattach and he cannot die. To lift the curse, he vows to kill a thousand evil men.

How it works

Rin Asano, a girl whose father was murdered and mother taken by a group of swordsmen called the Ittō-ryū, hires Manji as her bodyguard for revenge. Their journey through Edo-period Japan brings them into conflict with the Ittō-ryū, led by the charismatic Anotsu Kagehisa, who wants to destroy the old schools of swordsmanship, and with the government forces who hunt them all.

The art

Samura's art is one of the series' great strengths. He alternates between rough pencil sketches, detailed ink drawing and sudden explosions of motion, and his fights are fast, chaotic and bloody. His characters wear a mix of period clothing and anachronistic style, giving the world a punk edge.

Why it matters

It is one of the most admired samurai manga, praised for its art and its moral complexity: almost every swordsman has a reason, and revenge is never simple. Its English edition won an Eisner Award in 2000, and Takashi Miike adapted it as a film in 2017.

How the story is divided

The early volumes are a series of fights with members of the Ittō-ryū, each a duel with a swordsman who has his own story. The middle of the series follows Rin's journey alone to find Anotsu, and her growing doubt about revenge, while Manji is captured by the shogunate and used in experiments on the bloodworms. The last volumes bring all the factions together for a final battle, followed by an epilogue many years later.

Adaptations

Bee Train's anime (2008) adapted the early volumes, and Liden Films' Blade of the Immortal (2019) the whole story. Takashi Miike's live-action film appeared in 2017.

title: Emma
synopsis: In Victorian London, a quiet maid and the son of a wealthy merchant family fall in love across the barriers of class. Filed under 5, the turn.
body:
5Reduced, this title gives 5. It sits on The Turn with the rest of a turn.

What it is

Kaoru Mori's Emma ran in Enterbrain's Comic Beam from 2002, with its main story ending in 2006 and further stories about its characters continuing until 2008. It was collected in 10 volumes. Emma is a maid working for a retired governess in London at the end of the nineteenth century. William Jones, the heir to a newly rich merchant family and a former pupil of her employer, visits and falls in love with her.

How it works

The romance is slow and restrained. William's family expects him to marry into the aristocracy, and the gap between a maid and a gentleman is enormous. Emma is reserved and practical, and the story follows both of them as they decide what they are willing to give up.

The detail

Mori is famous for her love of Victorian Britain, and the series is full of carefully researched detail: costume, servants' work, households, trains, the Crystal Palace. The lives of the servants are given as much care as those of their employers.

Why it matters

It received an Excellence Prize at the Japan Media Arts Festival and was adapted as an anime in 2005. It is one of the most admired historical romances in manga and the work that first showed the patient, detailed style Mori developed further in A Bride's Story.

How the story is divided

The first volumes are the meeting of Emma and William, the death of her employer, and William's family's opposition. Emma leaves London and goes into service at a great German family's house in the countryside, and the middle of the series follows her new life and William's attempts to find her. The last volumes bring them back together against both families' opposition. The final three volumes are side stories about other characters, among them William's family and the servants.

Adaptations

Pierrot's anime ran for two seasons (2005 and 2007).

title: Ah! My Goddess
synopsis: An unlucky college student dials a wrong number and reaches a goddess, who grants him a wish, and he wishes that she would stay with him forever. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3Title sums to 48 and reduces to 3 — The Telling, where the reference files an act of telling.

What it is

Kōsuke Fujishima's Ah! My Goddess ran in Kodansha's Monthly Afternoon from 1988 to 2014 and was collected in 48 volumes. Keiichi Morisato is a shy, unlucky engineering student who lives in a cramped men's dormitory. Trying to order food by phone, he accidentally calls the Goddess Relief Office, and a goddess named Belldandy appears in his room to grant him one wish. Half joking, he wishes that a goddess like her would stay with him forever. The wish is granted.

How it works

Keiichi and Belldandy move into an old temple and are soon joined by her sisters: Urd, a seductive troublemaker, and Skuld, a young inventor who resents Keiichi. Most stories are comedy episodes about magic, mechanics and misunderstandings, while longer arcs involve demons, rival gods and the system of heaven itself.

The craft

Fujishima is a devoted motorcycle and car enthusiast, and the machines Keiichi rebuilds with his university motor club are drawn with great precision. His art evolved enormously over the long run, from rounded 1980s figures to an elegant, detailed style.

Why it matters

It is a classic of the gentle romantic comedy, with a devoted couple and very little conflict between them. Its anime adaptations, beginning with a 1993 original video series, made Belldandy an icon, and the series influenced many later stories in which a magical girl moves in with an ordinary young man.

How it is organised

Most of the series is episodic, but a few long arcs mark its course: Urd and Skuld's arrival; the demon Mara's repeated schemes; visits from heaven's other gods and goddesses; Keiichi's trials to prove he is worthy of a goddess; and, in the last volumes, a test that decides whether their bond can survive the rules of heaven. The ending settles the relationship that has run unresolved for twenty-six years.

Adaptations

A five-part OVA (1993) was followed by the short comedy The Adventures of Mini-Goddess (1998), a film (2000) and two television seasons (2005–2006).

title: Shaman King
synopsis: A laid-back boy who can see spirits enters a tournament held every five hundred years to decide the king of all shamans. 43 in the letters, reducing to 7.
body:
7Title sums to 43 and reduces to 7 — The Inquiry, where the reference files an open question.

What it is

Hiroyuki Takei's Shaman King ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1998 to 2004 and was collected in 32 volumes. Yoh Asakura is a relaxed, easygoing boy from a family of shamans, people who can see and communicate with spirits. He moves to Tokyo with the ghost of a samurai who died six hundred years earlier, Amidamaru, who becomes his partner in battle.

How it works

Every five hundred years, shamans from around the world fight in the Shaman Fight to decide who will become the Shaman King, able to reshape the world. Shamans fight by merging with their spirits, and each has a distinct style drawn from a different culture or religion. Yoh's strict fiancée, Anna, trains him, and he gathers friends from around the world, while his twin brother Hao threatens to win and destroy humanity.

Its ending

The original serialisation ended abruptly in 2004. Takei finished the story in a complete edition published in 2008 and 2009, adding the final chapters he had planned, and later wrote sequels.

Why it matters

It was one of Jump's major hits around 2000, and its anime, from 2001, and a remake in 2021 brought it to audiences worldwide. Its idea of fighting through partnerships with spirits, and its celebration of many cultures, are its lasting signatures.

How the story is divided

The early volumes are Yoh's first fights in Tokyo, where he meets the friends who will follow him, among them Ren Tao and Horohoro, and the preliminary rounds of the Shaman Fight. The story then moves to America, where the participants journey to the tournament's site in search of the Patch Village. The final part is the tournament itself and the war with Hao, the shaman reborn every five hundred years, which the original serialisation cut short and the complete edition finished.

Sequels and adaptations

Takei continued the world in Shaman King: Flowers (2012–2014), about Yoh's son Hana, and The Super Star (2018–2024), and other artists have drawn spin-offs. The 2001 anime (64 episodes) departed from the manga with its own ending. The 2021 remake by Bridge adapted the complete story in 52 episodes. The manga has passed 41 million copies.

title: Fairy Tail
synopsis: A young wizard joins a rowdy, close-knit guild of magic users and takes on jobs, rivals and dark guilds alongside a fire-eating dragon slayer. 47 in the letters, reducing to 11.
body:
11The letters of this title total 47, an 11 — the number of inspiration, tension, and heightened awareness.

What it is

Hiro Mashima's Fairy Tail ran in Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine from 2006 to 2017 and was collected in 63 volumes. In the kingdom of Fiore, wizards belong to guilds that take on jobs for pay. Lucy Heartfilia, a young celestial wizard who can summon spirits with magical keys, dreams of joining Fairy Tail, the most notorious guild of all. She is brought there by Natsu Dragneel, a fire-eating dragon slayer, and his flying blue cat, Happy.

How it works

The series alternates between comic jobs and long arcs against dark guilds, tournaments and ancient dragons. Each guild member has a distinctive magic, and the story places great weight on loyalty: when one member is hurt, the whole guild goes to war. Natsu, Lucy, the ice wizard Gray and the armoured swordswoman Erza form its central team.

The appeal

Mashima's art is bright and energetic, and the series is driven by friendship, found family and big emotional speeches. It does not aim for subtlety, and its directness was a large part of its popularity.

Why it matters

It was one of the most popular shōnen series of its time, especially outside Japan, and its long-running anime made it a gateway to manga for many readers. Mashima followed it with Edens Zero.

How the story is divided

The early arcs follow Lucy's first jobs and a series of battles with dark guilds. The Phantom Lord arc, a war between guilds, shows the guild's loyalty at its fiercest, and the Tower of Heaven arc tells Erza's past. The Tenrou Island arc ends with a seven-year time skip, after which the Grand Magic Games, a tournament between guilds, takes up several volumes. The last arcs are the war with Tartaros, a guild of demons, and the war with the Alvarez Empire, led by Zeref, the dark wizard behind much of the story.

Adaptations and sequel

The anime, by A-1 Pictures with Satelight and later Bridge, ran for 328 episodes from 2009 to 2019 and adapted the whole manga, with two films. The story continues in Fairy Tail: 100 Years Quest, written and storyboarded by Mashima and drawn by Atsuo Ueda, which began in 2018 and was adapted as an anime in 2024.

What it is

Atsushi Ōkubo's Soul Eater ran in Square Enix's Monthly Shōnen Gangan from 2004 to 2013 and was collected in 25 volumes. In Death City, Lord Death runs an academy for two kinds of students: weapons, people who can transform into blades, guns and other arms, and meisters, who wield them. Maka Albarn, a serious, studious meister, is partnered with Soul Eater, a laid-back boy who becomes a scythe.

How it works

To turn Soul into a Death Scythe, a weapon worthy of Lord Death himself, the pair must collect the souls of 99 evil humans and one witch. They train and fight alongside their classmates, including the loud ninja Black Star and Death's own son, Death the Kid, who is obsessed with symmetry. The series grows into a war against witches and an ancient being of madness.

The style

Ōkubo's art is gothic and playful, with grinning moons and suns, sharp shapes and fashionable characters. Madness, fear and courage are central themes, and the comedy and horror sit side by side.

Why it matters

Its 2008 anime by Studio Bones made it a worldwide hit, and its partnership between weapon and wielder, where each relies on the other's soul, is its most memorable idea. Ōkubo went on to create Fire Force.

How the story is divided

The early chapters are separate missions as Maka and Soul, Black Star and Tsubaki, and Kid and his twin pistols hunt souls. The story turns when the witch Medusa sets the demon god Asura free from beneath the academy, and madness begins to spread across the world. The middle volumes are a war between the academy and the witches, and a series of raids to recover the Kishin's allies. In the last part, the academy and the witches make an uneasy alliance and travel to the moon to face Asura.

Adaptations

Bones' anime (2008–2009) ran for 51 episodes and ends with its own story, before the manga's second half. A spin-off, Soul Eater Not!, followed in 2011–2014 and was adapted as an anime in 2014.

Reading it today

Complete in 25 volumes. Readers who know only the anime will find the manga's ending entirely different, and its connection to Fire Force rewarding.

title: Wandering Son
synopsis: Two transgender children, a boy who wants to be a girl and a girl who wants to be a boy, grow up together from primary school to adulthood. 62 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8The letters of this title total 62, an 8 — the number of money, authority, and the machinery of ambition.

What it is

Takako Shimura's Wandering Son ran in Enterbrain's Comic Beam from 2002 to 2013 and was collected in 15 volumes. Shūichi Nitori is a gentle fifth-grader, assigned male at birth, who wants to be a girl. Yoshino Takatsuki, a new classmate, is assigned female and wants to be a boy. They recognise something in each other and become close friends.

How it works

The story follows them and their classmates from primary school through puberty to the end of high school. Puberty brings changes that both dread. Shūichi experiments with dressing as a girl in public and faces the reactions of family, friends and strangers. Around them, other characters explore their own identities and feelings, including first loves.

The tone

Shimura writes with great tenderness and restraint. There is no melodrama: the series observes ordinary days, small cruelties and quiet acts of support. Its watercolour-soft art and gentle pace make it feel like a coming-of-age diary.

Why it matters

It is one of the most respected manga about transgender youth, praised for its honesty and care. It was adapted as an anime in 2011, and its English edition introduced many readers to Shimura's work, including the yuri romance Sweet Blue Flowers.

How the story is divided

The first volumes follow Shūichi and Yoshino in their last years of primary school, as they try out each other's clothes in secret and confide in a few friends, among them Saori Chiba, who loves Shūichi. Middle school brings uniforms, puberty and Shūichi's decision to go to school dressed as a girl, with its consequences. The last volumes follow them to high school and beyond, as each finds a way of living with who they are, and the story ends as they approach adulthood.

Adaptations

AIC Classic's anime (2011) begins in the middle-school years and covers only part of the story.

Reading it today

Complete in 15 volumes. Fantagraphics published the first eight volumes in English before the edition stopped, so the end is less available in English. Our entry on Takako Shimura covers her other work.

title: Wotakoi: Love Is Hard for Otaku
synopsis: Two office workers who are both secret otaku, a fujoshi and a hardcore gamer, start dating and try to be adults about it. 116 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Title sums to 116 and reduces to 8 — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

What it is

Fujita's Wotakoi: Love Is Hard for Otaku began as a webcomic posted on the illustration site pixiv in 2014, and was then serialised on Ichijinsha's web magazine Comic Pool until 2021, collected in 11 volumes. Narumi Momose has changed jobs to escape the fallout when her last boyfriend found out she was an otaku. At her new office she finds her childhood friend Hirotaka Nifuji, a quiet, devoted gamer.

How it works

Narumi, a fujoshi who loves boys' love manga, and Hirotaka, who plays games every spare moment, start dating, mostly because neither has to hide anything from the other. The episodes are short comic scenes from their relationship, their hobbies and their workplace, along with another couple, their colleagues Hanako and Tarō, who are also otaku.

The comedy

The series is full of fan in-jokes: game terms, convention habits, the particular language of BL fans. But its heart is an adult relationship between two people who are comfortable with each other, and it treats the characters' passions with affection rather than mockery.

Why it matters

It is a well-known example of a manga that began on pixiv and became a major hit. Its 2018 anime and 2020 live-action film made it popular with adult fans who saw themselves in it.

How it is organised

Each chapter is a short comic scene, often only a few pages, and the series has no single plot. Over its run, Narumi and Hirotaka move from dating as a convenience to a real partnership, Hanako and Tarō's arguments reveal their own devotion, and Hirotaka's younger brother, Naoya, joins the story with a friend who hides her own interests. The last volumes look further into the couples' futures.

Adaptations

A-1 Pictures' anime (2018) adapted the early volumes, with OVAs following. A live-action film appeared in 2020.

Reading it today

Complete in eleven volumes. Its short episodes make it easy to read a few at a time, and many readers do so on breaks from work, just as its characters would.

title: Erased
synopsis: A struggling manga artist who is sometimes sent back in time to prevent disasters is thrown back eighteen years to save a classmate from a serial killer. 25 in the letters, reducing to 7.
body:
7Reduced, this title gives 7. It sits on The Inquiry with the rest of an open question.

What it is

Kei Sanbe's Erased, whose Japanese title means "the town where only I am missing", ran in Kadokawa's Young Ace from 2012 to 2016. Satoru Fujinuma is a 29-year-old manga artist who delivers pizzas to make ends meet. He has a strange ability he calls Revival: when something terrible is about to happen, he is sent back a few minutes in time and can prevent it.

How it works

When his mother is murdered and he is blamed, Revival throws Satoru back eighteen years, to 1988, into his eleven-year-old body in a snowy town in Hokkaido. That winter, a classmate, Kayo Hinazuki, was abducted and killed, the first of a series of murders. Satoru realises that if he can save her, he may change everything that followed.

The heart

The mystery of the killer drives the plot, but the most moving parts are about Kayo, who is abused by her mother, and Satoru's efforts as a child, with an adult's mind, to protect her and befriend her. The series treats child abuse and loneliness with seriousness.

Why it matters

It was adapted as an anime and a live-action film in 2016 and as a Netflix series in 2017. Unusually for a time-travel thriller, its emotional centre is not the killer's identity but the slow work of making one neglected child safe.

How the story is divided

The first part is Satoru's return to 1988 and his efforts to save Kayo, with the help of his friends and his mother. When he fails, he is thrown back to the present, then returns again to try once more. The second part takes place in the present after the past has changed, and leads to the killer's identity and a final confrontation on a rooftop. The ninth volume, Erased Re, collects side stories told from other characters' points of view.

Adaptations

A-1 Pictures' anime (2016) changed the second half. A live-action film appeared in 2016 and a Netflix series, which follows the manga's ending, in 2017.

Reading it today

Complete in eight volumes plus Erased Re. Readers who know the anime should read the manga's second half, which is very different.

title: The Disastrous Life of Saiki K.
synopsis: A boy born with every psychic power imaginable wants only one thing: to be left alone and live a normal, unremarkable life. Read from the telling, as a 3.
body:
3Filed under 3. The Telling takes an act of telling, and this entry is renders one.

What it is

Shūichi Asō's The Disastrous Life of Saiki K. ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2012 to 2018 and was collected in 26 volumes. Kusuo Saiki was born with every psychic power: telepathy, telekinesis, teleportation, X-ray vision and more. He could rule the world. Instead, he finds his powers exhausting and wants only to live an unremarkable life, keep a low profile at school and eat coffee jelly.

How it works

Each chapter is a short comic episode in which Saiki's plans for a quiet life are wrecked by his classmates: the cheerful idiot Nendō, whose mind Saiki cannot read because he thinks nothing; the chūnibyō Kaidō, who believes he fights a secret war; and Teruhashi, the perfect girl who cannot believe he is not in love with her. Saiki's deadpan inner monologue narrates his suffering.

The joke

The series inverts the power fantasy. Saiki's powers make life worse, not better: reading every thought is noisy and disappointing, and every miracle makes it harder to be ordinary. He constantly uses godlike abilities for trivial ends.

Why it matters

It runs the psychic-hero fantasy backwards: every power is a nuisance, and the comedy is a near-god trying to pass as ordinary. Its anime, from 2016, became popular internationally, and it was adapted as a live-action film in 2017.

How it is organised

Almost every chapter is complete in itself, but the cast grows steadily: Toritsuka, a classmate who can see ghosts; Mikoto Aiura, a self-proclaimed psychic; Kusuke, Saiki's genius older brother, who is determined to beat him; and Saiki's doting, oblivious parents. Running jokes, such as Teruhashi's certainty that every boy must fall for her, build over years. The final arc turns to Saiki's attempt to rid himself of his powers for good.

Adaptations

J.C.Staff and Egg Firm's anime ran for two seasons (2016 and 2018), followed by a short final arc and Saiki K.: Reawakened (2019) on Netflix. A live-action film appeared in 2017.

Reading it today

Complete in 26 volumes, it can be read in any order. Our glossary entry on chūnibyō explains Kaidō's affliction.

title: Gaku
synopsis: A cheerful volunteer lives on the slopes of the Japanese Alps and rescues climbers in trouble, alive or dead. Filed under 4, the structure.
body:
4Title sums to 13 and reduces to 4 — The Structure, where the reference files a structure.

What it is

Shinichi Ishizuka's Gaku ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Original from 2003 to 2012 and was collected in 18 volumes. Sanpo Shimazaki is a climber who has climbed mountains all over the world. He now lives in a tent in Japan's Northern Alps and works as a volunteer with the local mountain rescue, bringing down climbers who are lost, injured or dead.

How it works

Most chapters follow one rescue and the people involved: a father and son, a lone climber, a group who ignored the weather. Some are saved and some are not. Sanpo greets everyone, living or dead, with the same words of encouragement, and never blames the climbers for loving the mountains. A young police officer, Kumi Shiina, joins the rescue team and learns from him.

The mountains

Ishizuka, a climber himself, draws the Alps with care in every season, and shows both their beauty and their danger: avalanches, storms and falls. The series is honest about death, but its tone is warm, built around Sanpo's love of the mountains and of people.

Why it matters

It won the first Manga Taishō in 2008 and the Shogakukan Manga Award, and was adapted as a live-action film in 2011. Few manga treat death as plainly: the mountain is not an enemy, and nobody is punished for having climbed it.

How it is organised

Most chapters are rescues, each with a different climber. Across the series, Kumi grows from a nervous newcomer into a capable rescuer, and Sanpo's own past is gradually revealed. The final volumes take Sanpo back to the Himalayas, and end with a climb that changes what the series means.

A live-action film, starring Shun Oguri, appeared in 2011.

title: Blue Giant
synopsis: A high-school boy in Sendai teaches himself the tenor saxophone by a river every night, determined to become the world's greatest jazz player. Filed under 1, the opening.
body:
1Title sums to 37 and reduces to 1 — The Opening, where the reference files a first move.

What it is

Shinichi Ishizuka's Blue Giant ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic from 2013 to 2016 and was collected in 10 volumes, followed by sequels set in Europe and America. Dai Miyamoto is a basketball-playing high-school student in Sendai who falls in love with jazz. He buys a tenor saxophone and practises alone by the riverbank every night, in all weathers, until his playing is loud and raw and impossible to ignore.

How it works

After school, Dai moves to Tokyo and forms a trio with a gifted, arrogant pianist, Yukinori Sawabe, and a beginner drummer, his friend Shunji Tamada. The story follows the band from empty clubs to their first real audiences. Each performance is drawn as an event, and the story is told partly through interviews with people who knew Dai, looking back from the future.

The challenge

The series has to show music that cannot be heard. Ishizuka does it through the players' bodies, sweat and faces, through the reactions of listeners and through bold, expressive lines that seem to burst from the instrument. Many readers have said they could hear the playing.

Why it matters

It is one of the great music manga, and it drew new readers to jazz. Its 2023 animated film, with music by the pianist Hiromi, was a hit, and the sequels Blue Giant Supreme and Blue Giant Explorer follow Dai abroad.

The series in order

The story continues across four series in Big Comic. Blue Giant (2013–2016, 10 volumes) covers Sendai and Tokyo. Blue Giant Supreme (2016–2020, 11 volumes) follows Dai to Germany and across Europe, where he forms a new band. Blue Giant Explorer (2020–2023, 9 volumes) takes him across the United States, and Blue Giant Momentum, which began in 2023, brings him to New York.

Adaptations and recognition

The animated film (2023), with music by Hiromi Uehara, won the Japan Academy Film Prize for best music. The first series won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 2017.

title: Princess Jellyfish
synopsis: A shy jellyfish fanatic in an all-women house of otaku befriends a glamorous stranger who turns out to be a cross-dressing politician's son. Filed under 11, the signal.
body:
11Reduced, this title gives 11. It sits on The Signal with the rest of a signal received early.

What it is

Akiko Higashimura's Princess Jellyfish ran in Kodansha's Kiss from 2008 to 2017 and was collected in 17 volumes. Tsukimi Kurashita is a shy young woman obsessed with jellyfish, who lives in Amamizukan, an old Tokyo boarding house occupied entirely by women otaku. They call themselves the Amars, "nuns", avoid fashionable people and men, and each has her own obsession, from trains to Japanese dolls to the Three Kingdoms.

How it works

One night Tsukimi is helped by a beautiful, stylish woman who turns out to be Kuranosuke Koibuchi, the son of a politician, who dresses as a woman because he loves fashion and to escape his family. When developers threaten to demolish Amamizukan, Kuranosuke helps the Amars fight back, including by turning Tsukimi's jellyfish into a fashion line.

The comedy

Higashimura's comedy is loud and affectionate, and the Amars' panic in the presence of attractive people is a running joke. But the series respects their passions, and its story is about finding confidence without abandoning who you are.

Why it matters

It won the Kodansha Manga Award for shōjo and was adapted as an anime (2010), a film (2014) and a television drama (2018). It is a well-loved example of josei comedy about otaku women.

How the story is divided

The early volumes are Kuranosuke's invasion of Amamizukan and the Amars' fight against the redevelopment of their neighbourhood. The middle of the series follows the creation of Jellyfish, the fashion brand built on Tsukimi's designs, and Kuranosuke's brother Shū, a shy politician's aide who falls for Tsukimi. The later volumes take the brand abroad with a powerful investor, and end with the Amars and the brothers settling their futures.

Adaptations

Brain's Base's anime (2010) adapted the early volumes. A live-action film appeared in 2014 and a Fuji TV drama in 2018.

title: Kuroko's Basketball
synopsis: An almost invisible player who was the hidden sixth man of a legendary team joins a new school to defeat his old teammates. 51 in the letters, reducing to 6.
body:
6The letters of this title total 51, a 6 — the number of care, community, and the weight of duty.

What it is

Tadatoshi Fujimaki's Kuroko's Basketball ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2008 to 2014 and was collected in 30 volumes. At Teikō Middle School, a team of five prodigies known as the Generation of Miracles dominated school basketball. They had a sixth member few people noticed: Tetsuya Kuroko, a small, plain player so easy to overlook that he can pass the ball without opponents seeing him.

How it works

In high school, Kuroko joins the new team at Seirin High and pairs with Taiga Kagami, a powerful player who has returned from America. Their goal is to defeat each of the Generation of Miracles, who have scattered to rival schools. Every rival has a near-superhuman skill, and Seirin must find ways to beat them through teamwork and strategy.

The style

The series turns basketball into a battle manga, with abilities that stretch realism, intense rivalries and dramatic matches. Its handsome, distinctive characters gave it a large audience among women as well as men.

Why it matters

It was a major hit, and its 2012 anime, stage plays and films spread its popularity. Fujimaki and events linked to the series were the targets of a long campaign of threats in 2012 and 2013, which ended with the arrest of a man who said he was jealous of Fujimaki's success.

How the story is divided

The first volumes are a practice match against Kaijō, Ryōta Kise's school, and the Inter-High qualifiers, where Seirin beats Shūtoku and its sharpshooter Midorima, then loses badly to Tōō and Daiki Aomine. After a summer of training, the Winter Cup takes up the second half: rematches with Tōō, then Yōsen and its giant centre Murasakibara, then Kaijō, and a final against Rakuzan, captained by Seijūrō Akashi, the leader of the Generation of Miracles.

Adaptations

Production I.G's anime ran for three seasons from 2012 to 2015 and adapted the whole manga. The sequel Extra Game was adapted as the film Last Game (2017).

title: D.Gray-man
synopsis: In an alternate nineteenth-century Europe, a young exorcist with a cursed eye and a weaponised arm fights the demons made from human grief. The title reduces to 11 — the signal.
body:
11Eleven — vision. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Katsura Hoshino's D.Gray-man began in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 2004, moved to Jump SQ in 2009 and has since appeared in its sister magazines, with long breaks. In an alternate nineteenth-century Europe, the Millennium Earl creates Akuma, demons made by tricking grieving people into calling back the souls of their dead. Only exorcists, who wield a mysterious substance called Innocence, can destroy them.

How it works

Allen Walker is a young exorcist whose left arm is itself a weapon of Innocence and whose cursed left eye lets him see the trapped souls inside Akuma. He joins the Black Order, the church organisation that fights the Earl, and the story follows its missions, its secrets and its war with the Noah, a family of humans with terrifying powers.

The style

Hoshino's art is gothic and elegant, with intricate costumes and beautifully designed characters. The story is dark, dealing with grief, manipulation and the Order's own cruelty, and it becomes increasingly complex.

Why it matters

It was a major Jump hit and has a devoted international following. Its long hiatuses have been due largely to Hoshino's health, and readers have followed it patiently for two decades.

How the story is divided

The early chapters are missions in which Allen hunts Akuma and recovers Innocence across Europe. The story grows with the Noah family's appearance and the voyage to Edo, then turns inward with an attack on the Black Order's headquarters and the revelation of the Fourteenth Noah, whose memories live inside Allen. In the later arcs, Allen flees the Order, which now sees him as a threat, and the story moves towards the history behind the Earl and the Order alike.

Adaptations

TMS Entertainment's anime ran for 103 episodes from 2006 to 2008, adding some original episodes. D.Gray-man Hallow (2016) adapts the next arc, but no further anime has been made. The manga has passed 29 volumes and 27 million copies.

Reading it today

Since 2018 it has run in the quarterly Jump SQ.Rise, so new chapters arrive slowly. Readers who know the anime will find much more story in the manga.

title: Kamisama Kiss
synopsis: A homeless high-school girl accidentally becomes the god of a run-down shrine, served by a proud and unwilling fox spirit. The title reduces to 9 — the closing.
body:
9Filed under 9. The Closing takes a completion, and this entry is hands on one.

What it is

Julietta Suzuki's Kamisama Kiss ran in Hakusensha's Hana to Yume from 2008 to 2016 and was collected in 25 volumes. Nanami Momozono's gambling father runs away, and she is evicted from her home. She helps a stranger, who in return gives her his home: a shrine. He was its land god, and by accepting it Nanami becomes the new god.

How it works

The shrine's familiar, Tomoe, a fox yōkai of great power and pride, refuses to serve a human girl until Nanami binds him with a kiss. As a god, Nanami must deal with yōkai, other gods and people's prayers, and the story moves between comic episodes and longer arcs, including a journey into Tomoe's past.

The romance

The heart of the series is the romance between Nanami and Tomoe, from irritation to devotion. Tomoe's past as a wild fox demon, and the impossibility of love between a yōkai and a human, give it weight.

Why it matters

It is a popular shōjo romance built on Japanese folklore, and its 2012 anime brought it a wide international audience. It shows the shōjo tradition of romance with supernatural beings, and the enduring appeal of the kitsune.

How the story is divided

The early volumes are comic episodes of Nanami's new life as a god: her first festival, a yōkai boy who follows her to school, and her rivalry with the snake familiar Mizuki. Longer arcs take her to a gathering of the gods in Izumo and to the underworld. The final and most important arc sends Nanami five hundred years into the past to save Tomoe from a curse, and reveals the history that made him who he is.

Adaptations

TMS Entertainment's anime ran for two seasons (2012 and 2015), with OVAs that adapt later chapters, including the journey into the past.

title: Yona of the Dawn
synopsis: A sheltered princess flees her palace after a coup and sets out to find the four legendary dragon warriors. Filed under 7, the inquiry.
body:
7Title sums to 61 and reduces to 7 — The Inquiry, where the reference files an open question.

What it is

Mizuho Kusanagi's Yona of the Dawn ran in Hakusensha's Hana to Yume from 2009 to 2025 and was collected in 48 volumes. Yona is the only daughter of the gentle king of Kōka, an imaginary kingdom inspired by ancient Korea and China. She is pampered and naive, and in love with her cousin Soo-won. On her sixteenth birthday she sees Soo-won kill her father and seize the throne.

How it works

Yona escapes with her bodyguard Hak, a fierce fighter who has loved her for years. A priest tells her of a legend: four warriors carrying the blood of dragons who once served the kingdom's founding king. Yona sets out to find them, and on her journey sees the poverty and suffering of her people for the first time.

The growth

Yona's transformation, from a sheltered princess into an archer and leader who fights for her people, is the centre of the story. Soo-won is not a simple villain: he turns out to be an able ruler, and the series asks what makes a good king.

Why it matters

It is one of the most loved shōjo fantasies of recent years, combining romance, action and politics. Its 2014 anime introduced it to many readers who wanted the story to continue, and its sixteen-year run made it one of Hana to Yume's longest-running series.

How the story is divided

The first arc is the coup and Yona's flight with Hak. The search for the four dragon warriors, the White, Blue, Green and Yellow Dragons, follows, and each recruitment is a story of its own. The party then travels the kingdom's provinces, fighting drug smugglers in a port, helping a starving village and a border war, while Soo-won consolidates his rule. The later arcs bring Yona and Soo-won face to face and turn to war with neighbouring countries, before the story ends in December 2025.

Adaptations

Pierrot's anime (2014–2015) covers only the early arcs in 24 episodes, with three OVAs. A sequel anime was announced in December 2025, when the manga ended.

title: Barakamon
synopsis: A proud young calligrapher who punched a critic is sent to a remote island to cool off, and is taken over by the village children. 31 in the letters, reducing to 4.
body:
4Reduced, this title gives 4. It sits on The Structure with the rest of a structure.

What it is

Satsuki Yoshino's Barakamon ran in Square Enix's magazines from 2009 to 2018, mostly in Monthly Shōnen Gangan, and was collected in 18 volumes. Seishū Handa is a talented, arrogant 23-year-old calligrapher. When an elderly exhibition curator calls his work textbook-perfect but lifeless, Handa punches him. His father sends him away to the Gotō Islands, off the coast of Nagasaki, to reflect.

How it works

Handa wants to work in peace, but the villagers will not leave him alone. A seven-year-old girl, Naru, adopts his house as her playground, followed by schoolgirls, teenagers and old neighbours who bring food and gossip. Each chapter is a small episode of island life: fishing, festivals, farming, a bath at a friend's house.

The art of living

Through the villagers, Handa learns to live and to write more freely, and his calligraphy changes. The title is a word in the local dialect meaning "energetic", and the series uses the dialect affectionately.

Why it matters

Its 2014 anime was popular, and it is a favourite example of the rural healing story, in which a city person finds themselves in the countryside. Yoshino also wrote a prequel, Handa-kun, about Handa's school days.

How it is organised

Each chapter is an episode of Handa's life on the island, from fishing and rice planting to the village festival and the funeral of an elder. Small threads build across the series: his preparations for a calligraphy exhibition, which tests what he has learned on the island, and his choice, after a return to Tokyo, to live on the island permanently. The final volumes follow his first years as a resident and Naru's growing up.

Adaptations and spin-off

Kinema Citrus' anime (2014) adapted the early volumes. Handa-kun (2013–2016), a prequel about Handa's high-school days, was adapted as an anime in 2016.

title: Sweetness & Lightning
synopsis: A widowed teacher who cannot cook learns to make real meals for his small daughter, with the help of one of his students. Filed under 4, the structure.

What it is

Gido Amagakure's Sweetness & Lightning ran in Kodansha's Good! Afternoon from 2013 to 2018 and was collected in 12 volumes. Kōhei Inuzuka is a high-school mathematics teacher whose wife has died, leaving him alone with their small daughter, Tsumugi. He cannot cook and feeds her on convenience-store meals.

How it works

Tsumugi meets Kotori Iida, a student of Kōhei's whose mother runs a restaurant but is rarely there. The three begin to cook together in the restaurant's kitchen, and each chapter follows a single dish, from rice to gyōza to hamburger steak, with a recipe. Kotori is afraid of knives, Kōhei is clumsy, and Tsumugi wants to help.

Grief and comfort

The series is gentle, but it is also about grief. Cooking becomes a way for Kōhei to care for Tsumugi and to rebuild a home. Meals are moments of connection, and the series shows how food brings people together.

Why it matters

Few cooking manga are so plainly about the person being fed: each recipe is a step in a widowed father learning to make a home. Its 2016 anime was widely praised.

How it is organised

Each chapter is built around a dish and a recipe, cooked by the three and then eaten together. The series moves slowly through Tsumugi's years at nursery school and the start of primary school, Kotori's last years of high school and Kōhei's growing confidence as a cook and a father. Its later chapters touch on Kōhei's grief more directly, and end with a look at the characters' future.

title: Food Wars!
synopsis: The son of a diner cook enrols in an elite culinary school where students settle disputes in cooking duels. Filed under 11, the signal.
body:
11Reduced, this title gives 11. It sits on The Signal with the rest of a signal received early.

What it is

Food Wars!, written by Yūto Tsukuda and drawn by Shun Saeki, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2012 to 2019 and was collected in 36 volumes. Its recipes were developed with the chef Yuki Morisaki. Sōma Yukihira has grown up cooking at his father's small diner. When his father closes it to work abroad, he sends Sōma to Tōtsuki, an elite culinary academy where only a tiny fraction of students graduate.

How it works

At Tōtsuki, disputes are settled by shokugeki, formal cooking duels judged on a single dish. Sōma, cocky and inventive, takes on the academy's elite, including Erina Nakiri, whose "God Tongue" can judge any flavour. The series follows exams, tournaments and finally a struggle over the school itself.

The style

Each duel is staged like a battle manga fight, with dishes developed and explained in detail. When judges taste a great dish, they react with ecstatic, often sexualised visions, a running joke that became the series' trademark.

Why it matters

It turned the cooking manga into a battle manga, and its 2015 anime was a major hit. Its recipes are real and cookable, and many readers have tried them.

How the story is divided

The series moves through Tōtsuki's trials: the entrance test, a brutal training camp, the Autumn Elections tournament, the Stagiaire, in which students work in real restaurants, and the Moon Banquet Festival. Its longest arc begins when Erina's father, Azami, takes over the school and abolishes free cooking; Sōma and his friends answer with a team shokugeki for the school's future. The final arc, The BLUE, a world tournament for young chefs, was shorter and divided readers.

J.C.Staff's anime ran for five seasons from 2015 to 2020 and adapted the story to its end, with changes in the last season.

title: Oishinbo
synopsis: A lazy newspaper journalist with a perfect palate builds an "Ultimate Menu" of Japanese food, while feuding with his tyrannical gourmet father. Read from the opening, as a 1.
body:
1One — initiative. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Oishinbo, written by Tetsu Kariya and drawn by Akira Hanasaki, ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1983 and was collected in more than a hundred volumes before going on hiatus in 2014. Shirō Yamaoka is an idle, cynical reporter at the Tōzai News, but he has an extraordinary knowledge of food and an impeccable sense of taste. The paper assigns him, with his colleague Yūko Kurita, to create the "Ultimate Menu", a collection of the finest dishes in Japan.

How it works

Each chapter centres on a dish, an ingredient or a problem: a restaurant in trouble, a dispute between chefs, a family meal gone wrong. Yamaoka solves it through knowledge of food, explaining in detail how ingredients are grown, prepared and cooked. His great rival is his estranged father, Yūzan Kaibara, a famous artist and gourmet who creates a competing "Supreme Menu" for another newspaper, and their contests run through the series.

The arguments

Oishinbo has strong opinions about food: it attacks additives, mass production and pretension, and praises seasonal, local and traditional cooking. It also became political, and in 2014 a story showing characters with nosebleeds after visiting the Fukushima nuclear plant caused a national controversy.

Why it matters

It is the great gourmet manga and did much to shape how Japanese readers thought about food in the boom years of the 1980s. Its anime and its influence on later food manga, food television and restaurant culture were enormous.

title: What Did You Eat Yesterday?
synopsis: A careful, thrifty lawyer cooks dinner every night for his partner, a cheerful hairdresser, in a quiet story of a gay couple's daily life. 98 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Reduced, this title gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

What it is

Fumi Yoshinaga's What Did You Eat Yesterday? has run in Kodansha's Morning since 2007. Shirō Kakei is a lawyer in his forties in Tokyo: precise, frugal and private about his sexuality at work. Every evening he goes home and cooks dinner for his partner, Kenji Yabuki, a warm, expressive hairdresser who is much more open about who he is.

How it works

Each chapter follows a day in their lives and ends with a meal. Shirō's cooking is shown step by step, as real, practical recipes, with attention to cost, seasons and leftovers. Around the meals, the series follows their relationship, their work, Shirō's parents' struggle to accept him and their friends, including another gay couple.

The tone

The series is quiet and realistic. It is not about coming out or crisis, but about the ordinary days of a long relationship, and about ageing together. Its frankness about money, family and discrimination is gentle but clear.

Why it matters

It is a much-loved work of everyday life and one of the most widely read manga about a gay couple in Japan. Its 2019 television drama and 2021 film were big successes, and its recipes have been cooked by many readers.

How it is organised

There are no arcs; time passes slowly and steadily across the volumes, and the characters age with it. Small threads run through the whole: Shirō's visits to his parents, who slowly come to accept Kenji; Kenji's jealousy and his wish to be introduced as Shirō's partner; their friendship with Kayoko, a housewife who shares bulk purchases with Shirō; and the couple's worries about illness, old age and what will happen to the one left behind.

Adaptations

TV Tokyo's drama (2019), a New Year special (2020), a film (2021) and a second season (2023) have all been popular. The manga won the Kodansha Manga Award in 2019 and has 24 volumes.

Reading it today

Still running. Many readers cook the recipes, which are practical and inexpensive. Our guide to manga about food and cooking places it among other food stories.
