title: The Prince of Tennis
synopsis: A cocky twelve-year-old tennis prodigy joins a powerful middle-school team and takes on rivals with ever more impossible techniques. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11Eleven — vision. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Takeshi Konomi's The Prince of Tennis ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1999 to 2008 and was collected in 42 volumes, followed by The New Prince of Tennis in Jump SQ (2009–2026, 48 volumes). Ryōma Echizen, the son of a legendary player, returns from America and joins the tennis club at Seishun Academy, a middle school with a strong team. Though only a first-year, he is already brilliant, and arrogant with it.

How it works

Seishun's team, known as Seigaku, competes in district, regional and national tournaments against rival schools, each with its own star players and signature shots. Ryōma learns from his teammates, especially the captain, Kunimitsu Tezuka, and grows into a player who enjoys the game for its own sake.

The techniques

The series begins realistically, but its techniques become steadily more outrageous, until players seem able to split into copies, summon visions and send opponents flying. This escalation became a famous joke among fans, who enjoy it as spectacle.

Why it matters

It was a major hit, and its musical adaptation, from 2003, launched the modern 2.5D stage industry and the careers of many actors. Its large cast of handsome rivals gave it an especially strong following among women readers.

How the story is divided

The original series follows Seigaku through the tournaments of one school year: the district preliminaries, the Kantō regional tournament, with its rivalry against Hyōtei and the injury that sends Tezuka away for treatment, and the National Tournament, which ends with a final against Rikkai, the reigning champions. The New Prince of Tennis sends the best middle-school players to a training camp with high-school players for the under-17 national team, and then to a world cup against teams from around the world.

Adaptations

Trans Arts' anime ran for 178 episodes from 2001 to 2005, followed by OVAs that adapted the National Tournament, several anime series of The New Prince of Tennis and a 3DCG film, Ryoma! (2021). The stage musical has run since 2003.

title: Eyeshield 21
synopsis: A timid errand boy who became fast from running away from bullies is recruited, masked, as the star running back of a hopeless American football team. 47 in the letters, reducing to 11.
body:
11The letters of this title total 47, an 11 — the number of inspiration, tension, and heightened awareness.

What it is

Eyeshield 21, written by Riichirō Inagaki and drawn by Yūsuke Murata, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2002 to 2009 and was collected in 37 volumes. Sena Kobayakawa is a timid high-school student who has spent his life running errands for bullies. Running away from them has made him extraordinarily fast. Yōichi Hiruma, the demonic captain of Deimon High's tiny American football team, the Devil Bats, sees him run and forces him to join.

How it works

To hide his identity from rival teams, Sena plays in a green-visored helmet as the mysterious "Eyeshield 21". The Devil Bats begin with almost no players, and recruit misfits, from a sumo-sized lineman to a monkey-like receiver. The story follows them towards the Christmas Bowl, the high-school championship, against rivals with their own styles.

The sport

American football was little known in Japan, and the series explains its rules and tactics clearly, through games built around plays, deceptions and strategy. Hiruma, who blackmails and schemes to win, is one of Jump's most memorable characters.

Why it matters

It made a sport most of its readers had never watched clear from the first chapter, and introduced many to American football. Murata's art grew into the extraordinary detail he later brought to One-Punch Man, and its anime ran from 2005.

How the story is divided

The first volumes are the spring tournament, in which the Devil Bats recruit their team and face the powerful Ōjō White Knights, and lose. The team then goes to America for a training camp, crossing the desert from Texas to Las Vegas on foot, a march that remakes them. The autumn tournament is the series' heart, from Tokyo to the Kantō tournament, with matches against Ōjō, the Shinryūji Nagas and the Hakushū Dinosaurs. The last volumes are the Christmas Bowl against Teikoku and an epilogue at a youth world cup.

Adaptations

Gallop's anime ran for 145 episodes from 2005 to 2008 and ended before the Christmas Bowl.

Reading it today

Complete in 37 volumes. Our guide to how sports manga work explains its matches, and our entry on Riichirō Inagaki covers his later work.

title: xxxHolic
synopsis: A boy plagued by spirits works in a shop where a witch grants any wish, for a price. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11Eleven — vision. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

CLAMP's xxxHolic ran in Kodansha's Young Magazine from 2003 and finished in Bessatsu Shōnen Magazine in 2011, collected in 19 volumes. Kimihiro Watanuki, a high-school student, can see spirits, which are drawn to him and make his life miserable. One day he is pulled into a strange shop owned by Yūko Ichihara, a beautiful witch who grants wishes, always in exchange for something of equal value.

How it works

To pay for his wish to be free of spirits, Watanuki works for Yūko as a cook and cleaner. Each story brings a new customer with a wish, often connected to an obsession or addiction, the "holic" of the title, and Yūko's lessons about fate and price. Watanuki's quarrelsome friendship with a classmate, Dōmeki, whose presence drives spirits away, is a running thread.

The crossover

xxxHolic was published alongside CLAMP's Tsubasa: Reservoir Chronicle, and the two stories cross over, with characters travelling between them. The later volumes become darker and stranger.

Why it matters

It is one of CLAMP's most stylish works, drawn in a flat, elegant style inspired by traditional Japanese prints. Its anime adaptations, from 2006, and its live-action film (2022) brought it to new audiences.

How the story is divided

The first part is a series of customers' stories, each about a wish and its price, as Watanuki works off his debt. The stories gather around his own wish and what it would cost, his growing bond with Dōmeki and the girl Himawari, and the connection between Yūko's shop and Tsubasa's travellers. The later volumes turn on Yūko's disappearance, after which Watanuki takes over the shop and waits for her, unable to leave it, for many years.

Adaptations and sequel

Production I.G's anime ran for two seasons (2006 and 2008), and a film appeared in 2005. A television drama aired in 2013 and a live-action film by Mika Ninagawa in 2022. The sequel, xxxHolic: Rei, began in 2013, went on long hiatus, and resumed in 2025.

Reading it today

Complete in 19 volumes, and best read alongside Tsubasa: Reservoir Chronicle.

title: Gyo
synopsis: Fish on mechanical legs begin walking out of the sea, followed by a stench of death, and the invasion spreads across Japan. The title reduces to 2 — the pairing.
body:
2Filed under 2. The Pairing takes a negotiation, and this entry is answers one.

What it is

Junji Ito's Gyo ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 2001 to 2002 and was collected in 2 volumes. Tadashi and his girlfriend Kaori are on holiday in Okinawa when a small fish with insect-like metal legs scuttles out of the sea. Soon there are many more: sharks, squid and schools of fish, all walking on mechanical legs and giving off an overwhelming smell of rot.

How it works

The invasion spreads to Tokyo, and the reason for the walking fish is gradually revealed, connected to a weapon developed in the Second World War. The machines do not stop with fish. As the infection spreads, the story moves from strange to grotesque to apocalyptic.

The horror

Ito's horror depends on the absurd made real: a fish walking on legs is almost funny until it is everywhere. His detailed drawing of bodies being changed by machines is both disgusting and hard to forget, and the smell, constantly mentioned, makes the horror physical.

Why it matters

It is one of Ito's best-known works outside Uzumaki and Tomie, and a classic of body horror. Its short length makes it a common introduction to his work, and it was adapted as an animated film in 2012.

How the story is divided

The first volume is the invasion: the first walking fish in Okinawa, its spread to Tokyo, and Kaori's infection with the gas that drives the machines, which leaves her body bloated and foul. The second follows Tadashi's search for a cure through a ruined city, his uncle's research into the wartime weapon, and the spread of the machines to human beings, ending in a grim parade of the infected. The volumes usually also include two short stories, "The Sad Tale of the Principal Post" and "The Enigma of Amigara Fault", the second one of Ito's most famous.

Adaptations

Ufotable's animated film (2012) changes much of the story.

Reading it today

title: Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction
altTitles: デッドデッドデーモンズデデデデデストラクション
synopsis: Two schoolgirls go on with their lives in a Tokyo where a gigantic alien mothership has hung in the sky for three years. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3The letters of this title total 138, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

What it is

Inio Asano's Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 2014 to 2022 and was collected in 12 volumes. Three years earlier, an enormous alien mothership appeared over Tokyo, and a disaster killed many people. Since then it has simply hung in the sky. Smaller ships are sometimes shot down by the military, and people have learned to live with it.

How it works

Kadode Koyama and her best friend Ōran Nakagawa, a loud, eccentric girl, are high-school students who spend their days talking, playing games and going to cram school, while news of the "invaders" plays in the background. Gradually, the story widens to show the government, the media, protesters, conspiracy theorists and the aliens themselves, and the disaster that changed everything.

The satire

Asano uses the giant ship to satirise how society reacts to catastrophe: how quickly people adapt, how the media and government shape the story, and how ordinary life goes on. The series was widely read as a response to the 2011 earthquake and nuclear disaster.

Why it matters

It combines Asano's detailed, realistic art and his interest in disaffected young people with large-scale science fiction. It was adapted as a two-part animated film in 2024 and is one of the most ambitious works of his career.

How the story is divided

The first volumes are Kadode and Ōran's high-school lives under the ship, with flashbacks to their childhood and a gadget that Ōran's family inherited from a visitor. The middle of the series follows them to university and widens to show the aliens, who turn out to be small, frightened refugees, and the private military hunting them. The final volumes reveal the purpose of the mothership and a coming catastrophe, and bring Kadode and Ōran to a choice about the world.

Adaptations

Production +h.'s animated film was released in two parts in 2024, followed by a television version.

title: Sand Land
synopsis: A demon prince, his old servant and a human sheriff cross a desert world in an old tank to find a hidden source of water. Filed under 6, the care.
body:
6The letters of this title total 24, a 6 — the number of care, community, and the weight of duty.

What it is

Akira Toriyama's Sand Land ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 2000 for fourteen chapters and was collected in a single volume. In a world turned into desert, water is scarce and controlled by a greedy king who sells it at outrageous prices. Rao, an old sheriff, believes there must be a hidden spring, and asks for help from the demons who live nearby.

How it works

Beelzebub, the young demon prince, joins Rao along with his elderly servant Thief, and the three set off across the desert in a commandeered tank. They fight the king's army, which is led by a tank commander with a grudge, and discover that Rao has a secret past and that the king's monopoly hides a bigger lie.

Toriyama's machines

Toriyama loved drawing vehicles, and Sand Land is full of beautifully designed tanks, jeeps and aircraft. The story is light and funny, but it has a clear message about greed and the people who suffer from it.

Why it matters

It is a perfect example of Toriyama's later short works: complete, inventive and full of charm. It was adapted as an animated film in 2023, an anime series and a video game in 2024.

How the story is divided

The fourteen chapters follow a single journey: the start of the expedition, the theft of a tank from the royal army, a series of fights with the army's soldiers and its general, and the discovery of the spring and of what the king has done with the world's water. The story ends with Rao's past revealed and the desert beginning to change.

Adaptations

The CGI film (2023), by Sunrise, Kamikaze Douga and Anima, was followed by Sand Land: The Series on Disney+ in 2024, whose second half adds a new story, The Story of the Angel Hero, written by Toriyama himself. It was among the last works he completed before his death in March 2024. An action role-playing game by ILCA followed in April 2024.

Reading it today

A single volume, readable in an hour. Our entry on Akira Toriyama covers his other works.

title: Goodbye, Eri
synopsis: A boy films his dying mother on his phone, then meets a mysterious girl who wants him to make another film, in a story about how we remember the dead. Filed under 6, the care.
body:
6Reduced, this title gives 6. It sits on The Care with the rest of an obligation.

What it is

Tatsuki Fujimoto's Goodbye, Eri is a single long story of about two hundred pages, published on Shueisha's Shōnen Jump+ in 2022. Yūta, a boy whose mother is dying, has been asked by her to film her last days on his phone. The film he makes is screened at his school, and ends with him running away from the hospital as it explodes. His classmates mock it.

How it works

Yūta meets Eri, a strange girl who loved his film and wants him to make another, this time with her as the star. Almost the whole story is drawn as if seen through a phone camera, in rows of identical horizontal panels. As the story goes on, the reader can never be sure what is real and what is part of the film.

The questions

The story asks how we remember the people we lose, and whether making art about them is a way of loving them or of turning them into fiction. Its final pages change the meaning of what came before.

Why it matters

Coming after Look Back, it confirmed Fujimoto as a master of the long one-shot. Its phone-camera grid is one of the boldest formal choices in recent mainstream manga, and readers still argue over what its ending makes true.

How it is told

The story moves in layers. The first is Yūta's film about his mother and its humiliating screening. The second is his friendship with Eri, who teaches him to watch films and makes a new film with him. The third is what happens when Eri falls ill, and the fourth reveals, years later, what Yūta has done with his footage and with his memories. Each layer reframes the one before it, and the story ends with an image that can be read in more than one way.

Reading it today

A single volume, readable in under an hour; most readers reread it at once. Our entry on Look Back covers Fujimoto's previous one-shot, and our entry on Tatsuki Fujimoto his longer series.

title: They Were Eleven
synopsis: Ten candidates for a space academy are sent to survive on a derelict ship as their final exam, and find that there are eleven of them. 73 in the letters, reducing to 1.
body:
1The letters of this title total 73, a 1 — the number of beginnings, leadership, and the will to act alone.

What it is

Moto Hagio's They Were Eleven was published in Shogakukan's Bessatsu Shōjo Comic in 1975. In the far future, candidates for a prestigious space academy face a final test: teams of ten are sent to a drifting spaceship and must survive there for fifty-three days without calling for help. When one team boards their ship, they find there are eleven of them.

How it works

No one knows who the extra person is, and everyone suspects everyone else. As the ship's systems fail and a disease threatens them, the candidates, who come from many planets and cultures, must cooperate despite their fear. The mystery of the eleventh member and the struggle to survive drive the story.

Frol

Among the candidates is Frol, from a planet where people are born without a fixed sex and decide in adulthood. Frol wants to become a man, but faces pressure to become a woman, and the story treats the question with sympathy and humour.

Why it matters

It is a classic of shōjo science fiction and one of the works that showed girls' manga could tell serious, ambitious genre stories. It won the Shogakukan Manga Award together with Hagio's The Poe Clan, and was adapted as an animated film in 1986.

How it is told

The story is short and tightly built, published as a single long work. The first part is the arrival on the derelict ship and the discovery of the eleventh person; suspicion falls first on the most unusual candidates, among them Frol and the haughty King Mayang. The middle part brings the ship's failures and a deadly fever, and the last part reveals who the eleventh is and why, in a solution that turns the test's purpose upside down.

Adaptations

An animated film appeared in 1986, and the story has been staged several times.

Reading it today

Short enough to read in one sitting. Our guide to the Year 24 Group places it among the works that changed shōjo manga, and our entry on The Poe Clan covers Hagio's other prize-winning work.

title: Your Lie in April
synopsis: A piano prodigy who stopped being able to hear his own playing is pulled back to music by a free-spirited young violinist. The title reduces to 4 — the structure.
body:
4Filed under 4. The Structure takes a structure, and this entry is frames one.

What it is

Naoshi Arakawa's Your Lie in April ran in Kodansha's Monthly Shōnen Magazine from 2011 to 2015 and was collected in eleven volumes. Kōsei Arima was a child piano prodigy, drilled relentlessly by his mother. After her death he found he could no longer hear the notes he played, and he gave up performing.

The story

In his second year of middle school, Kōsei meets Kaori Miyazono, a violinist who plays competition pieces in her own wild, joyful way and ignores the judges. She drags him back on stage as her accompanist, and slowly, painfully, he begins to play again.

How it is drawn

Arakawa shows music through images: light, colour words, flowing panels and the faces of the audience. Performances take whole chapters, and the series is as much about what music feels like as about the characters.

Why it matters

It is one of the best-loved music manga, and a story about grief, youth and finding your own voice. Its 2014 anime adaptation brought it, and a great deal of classical music, to a wide audience, and it was also made into a live-action film.

How the story is divided

The story covers about a year, from one spring to the next. The first half brings Kōsei back to music: his accompaniment of Kaori at a violin competition, and his own return to piano competitions, where he faces the rivals he left behind as a child. The second half is about Kaori's illness, Kōsei's search for his own reason to play, and the letter that gives the title its meaning.

Adaptations

A-1 Pictures' anime (2014–2015) follows the manga closely and is famous for its performances, recorded by professional musicians. A live-action film followed in 2016, and a stage musical in 2022.

Reading it today

Complete in eleven volumes, it can be read in a weekend. Readers will want to listen to the pieces as they appear: Chopin, Beethoven, Saint-Saëns and Kreisler are all part of the story.

title: The Quintessential Quintuplets
synopsis: A poor, studious boy is hired to tutor five identical sisters who hate studying, and one of them, we know from the start, will become his bride. 122 in the letters, reducing to 5.
body:
5The letters of this title total 122, a 5 — the number of freedom, disruption, and restless movement.

What it is

Negi Haruba's The Quintessential Quintuplets ran in Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine from 2017 to 2020 and was collected in fourteen volumes. Fūtarō Uesugi is a top student from a poor family. He takes a well-paid job as a private tutor, and discovers that his pupils are five identical sisters, the Nakano quintuplets, all failing and none of them keen on him.

The sisters

Ichika, Nino, Miku, Yotsuba and Itsuki look alike but are very different people, and each slowly grows closer to Fūtarō in her own way. Their hair, voices and habits are carefully distinguished, and the sisters sometimes swap places to confuse him.

The mystery

The first chapter opens on Fūtarō's wedding years later, without showing which sister is the bride. That question turns a romantic comedy into a guessing game, and readers argued over the clues for the whole run.

Why it matters

It was one of the biggest romantic comedies of its time, and a definitive example of the multiple-heroine love story. It was adapted into an anime series in 2019 and an anime film in 2022.

How the story is divided

The 122 chapters move from Fūtarō's struggle to get the sisters to study at all, through school trips, exams and family crises, to the sisters' graduation and the reveal of the bride. Each sister has her own turning point in which her feelings become clear, and the series famously alternates its focus so that no one is ruled out until the end. The volume covers rotate between the five.

Adaptations

The anime ran for two seasons (2019 and 2021), with a change of studio between them, and concluded with a film in 2022 that adapts the final arc, followed by additional animated specials. Readers who want the full set of clues should read the manga: the film compresses the last volumes.

title: Blue Exorcist
synopsis: A boy who learns he is the son of Satan decides to become an exorcist and fight the demons whose blood he shares. Filed under 9, the closing.
body:

What it is

Kazue Katō's Blue Exorcist has run in Shueisha's Jump SQ since 2009. Rin Okumura is a hot-tempered teenager raised in a church by the priest Shirō Fujimoto, alongside his studious twin brother Yukio. When demons come for him, Rin learns the truth: he is a son of Satan, and the blue flames he carries are his father's power.

The story

After Shirō dies protecting him, Rin enrols at True Cross Academy to train as an exorcist, so that he can one day defeat Satan. He discovers that Yukio is already an exorcist, and his own teacher. His classmates must decide whether to trust someone who is, by birth, the thing they are training to fight.

Its world

The series mixes Christian demonology with Japanese religion and folklore. Exorcists specialise as swordsmen, gunners, healers, summoners or chanters, and the demon world mirrors the human one.

Why it matters

It is a popular, long-running battle series and a central title of Jump SQ. Its anime adaptation began in 2011 and has returned for several seasons.

How the story is divided

The opening volumes follow Rin's first year at True Cross Academy's exorcist cram school and the revelation of what he is to his classmates. The Kyoto arc, built around the theft of the Impure King's left eye, is the first long arc and the one many fans consider the series' best: it gives each classmate a family and a stake. Later arcs turn to the Illuminati, a secret organisation trying to open the way between the worlds, and to the past: how Rin and Yukio were born and what Shirō Fujimoto really did.

Adaptations

The first anime season (2011) caught up with the manga and invented its own ending, followed by a film in 2012. Kyoto Saga (2017) returned to the manga's story, and after a long gap the anime came back in 2024 with new seasons continuing from where the manga left off.

title: Black Clover
synopsis: In a world where everyone has magic, an orphan born with none at all sets out to become the Wizard King. Read from the turn, as a 5.
body:
5Five — change. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Yūki Tabata's Black Clover began in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 2015 and moved to the quarterly Jump GIGA in 2023, where it ended in 2026 after 392 chapters. Asta and Yuno are orphans, left at the same church on the same night, in the Clover Kingdom, where magic is part of everyday life. Yuno is a prodigy. Asta, uniquely, cannot use magic at all.

The story

At fifteen, each receives a grimoire. Yuno's has four leaves; Asta's is a battered five-leaf book holding anti-magic swords that cancel spells. Both join the Magic Knights, Asta in the Black Bulls, the rowdiest and least respected squad, and both race towards the same dream: becoming Wizard King.

The style

It is an unashamedly classic battle shōnen, built on rivalry, effort and teamwork, with a huge cast of squads and captains. Asta's refusal to give up, shouted at full volume, is the series' heart.

Why it matters

It kept the classic Jump formula of rivalry, effort and a single ranked goal running through a decade in which many of the magazine's hits moved away from it, and it finished the story it set out to tell. Its anime ran for 170 episodes from 2017 to 2021 and was followed by a film in 2023.

How the story is divided

The first arcs follow Asta and Yuno's entry into the Magic Knights and their first missions, fighting the Eye of the Midnight Sun, a group of rebels with a grudge against the kingdom. The middle of the series is a crisis inside the kingdom, when elves reincarnated in the bodies of the Magic Knights take over, followed by a war with the Spade Kingdom and its devil hosts, in which Asta learns to fight with the devil inside his grimoire. The final arc sets the knights against Lucius Zogratis, who plans to remake the world, and ends with Asta's dream decided.

Adaptations

Pierrot's anime ran for 170 episodes from 2017 to 2021, followed by the film Sword of the Wizard King (2023). A second season was announced in 2025 and premiered in October 2026. The manga has passed 25 million copies.

Reading it today

Complete in 38 volumes. The first season of the anime ends partway through the Spade Kingdom arc, so readers who know it should continue from there.

title: Buddha
synopsis: Osamu Tezuka's long retelling of the life of Siddhartha Gautama, mixing history, invention, humour and philosophy. 22 in the letters, with nothing left to reduce.
body:
22Title sums to 22 with nothing to reduce — The Edifice, where the reference files an edifice.

What it is

Osamu Tezuka's Buddha was serialised from 1972 to 1983, beginning in Ushio Publishing's Kibō no Tomo. It tells the life of Siddhartha Gautama, from his birth as a prince of the Shakya clan to his enlightenment and death.

How Tezuka tells it

Tezuka treats the history freely. He adds invented characters, such as the slave boy Chapra, who hides his caste to rise in the world, and the thief Tatta, who can enter the bodies of animals. Their stories run alongside Siddhartha's and show the cruelty of the caste system and the suffering the Buddha sets out to understand.

The tone

The series moves between battles, slapstick, anachronistic jokes and serious, beautiful passages about life, death and the connection of all living things. That mix is typical of Tezuka, and it makes a long religious epic easy to read.

Why it matters

It is one of Tezuka's major late works, alongside Phoenix and Black Jack, and it has introduced many readers worldwide to Buddhism. It was published in English by Vertical in eight volumes.

How the story is divided

The first part sets out the world before Siddhartha's birth through Chapra and Tatta, and through the monk Naradatta, punished for sacrificing animals by being made to live as one. The second follows Siddhartha's youth as a prince, his shock at age, sickness and death, and his departure from the palace. The third is his years as an ascetic and his enlightenment; the last follows his teaching, his disciples, among them Ananda, a former bandit, and the war that destroys his own Shakya clan, before his death.

Adaptations

Two animated films, in 2011 and 2014, adapted the early part of the story.

Reading it today

Complete, and in English collected by Vertical in eight volumes, which won Eisner Awards in 2004 and 2005. No knowledge of Buddhism is needed. Our entry on Osamu Tezuka covers his other epics.

title: Princess Knight
synopsis: A princess born with both a boy's and a girl's heart is raised as a prince to keep her kingdom's throne, in Osamu Tezuka's founding shōjo adventure. Read from the opening, as a 1.
body:
1One — initiative. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Osamu Tezuka's Princess Knight began in Kodansha's Shōjo Club in 1953. Through the mischief of a young angel, Tink, Princess Sapphire of Silverland is born with two hearts, a boy's and a girl's. Because only a male heir can inherit the throne, she is raised as a prince.

The story

Sapphire fences, rides and rules as a prince, while a wicked duke plots to expose her and put his own son on the throne. In secret, she is also a young woman who falls in love. Tink must retrieve the extra heart, and Sapphire faces witches, pirates and war.

Its sources

Tezuka grew up in Takarazuka, home of the all-female Takarazuka Revue, and its women playing men's roles shaped Sapphire. He also drew on fairy tales and Disney animation. He later redrew the story in Nakayoshi in the 1960s, and it became an anime in 1967.

Why it matters

It is one of the first story manga for girls, and a model for heroines who act, fight and choose. Its line runs directly to The Rose of Versailles and Sailor Moon.

Versions

Tezuka drew Princess Knight more than once. The first version ran in Shōjo Club from 1953 to 1956. A sequel, Twin Knight, about Sapphire's children, followed in 1958. A longer, redrawn version, which most modern editions use, ran in Nakayoshi from 1963 to 1966.

Adaptations

Mushi Production's anime ran for 52 episodes from 1967 to 1968, and the story has been adapted for the stage.

Reading it today

The redrawn version is complete in English. Our guide to the Year 24 Group and the reinvention of shōjo explains what came after it, and our entry on Osamu Tezuka covers his other works.

title: Magic Kaito
synopsis: A teenage magician discovers his murdered father was the phantom thief Kaitō Kid, and takes on the role to find the killers. Filed under 8, the ledger.
body:
8The letters of this title total 44, an 8 — the number of money, authority, and the machinery of ambition.

What it is

Gosho Aoyama's Magic Kaito began in Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday in 1987, before Detective Conan, and has appeared only occasionally since. Kaito Kuroba is a cocky high-school student and a gifted stage magician, like his late father, Tōichi.

The story

Kaito discovers a secret room in his house and learns that his father was the famous gentleman thief Kaitō Kid, and that his death on stage was no accident. He puts on the white suit and top hat himself, to draw out the criminal organisation that killed his father, which is hunting a legendary jewel.

The style

Each heist is a magic trick: misdirection, disguise and impossible escapes, played for fun more than danger. A police inspector and a detective rival try to catch him, and his childhood friend never suspects.

Why it matters

Kaitō Kid crossed into Detective Conan as Conan's recurring rival and became one of its most popular characters. Because the original series has so few chapters, readers mostly know Kid from those crossovers.

How to read it

There is no long plot. The chapters, published irregularly over more than thirty years, are separate heists, each with a trick at its centre, and a few longer threads: the organisation that killed Kaito's father, the jewel Pandora that they are seeking, the witch Akako, and the detective Saguru Hakuba. The latest volume collects chapters drawn decades after the first.

Adaptations

TMS Entertainment's Magic Kaito 1412 (2014–2015) adapted the manga's chapters together with Kid's appearances in Detective Conan and original episodes. Kid is the central figure of several Detective Conan films.

Reading it today

The few volumes can be read quickly. Readers who know Kid from Detective Conan will find a lighter, more comic version of him here. Our entry on Gosho Aoyama covers his other work.

title: Cross Game
synopsis: Years after a loss that marks them both, a boy pitches for Kōshien with the girl who was always his rival at his side. The title reduces to 1 — the opening.
body:
1A 1 by its title: leader & pioneer, and therefore the opening.

What it is

Mitsuru Adachi's Cross Game ran in Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 2005 to 2010 and was collected in seventeen volumes. Kō Kitamura grows up next door to the four Tsukishima sisters, whose family runs a batting centre. The second sister, Wakaba, is his closest friend, and everyone assumes they will end up together.

The story

When they are in fifth grade, Wakaba dies in an accident. In high school, Kō becomes a remarkable pitcher and sets out to fulfil her dream of seeing him play at Kōshien. Her younger sister Aoba, who was close to Wakaba and resents Kō, is just as good a pitcher, but as a girl she cannot play in official games.

The style

It is classic Adachi: quiet, understated and funny, with feelings shown in silences, glances and empty panels rather than said aloud. The baseball is tense, but the heart of it is grief and the slow bond between Kō and Aoba.

Why it matters

It is among Adachi's finest works, and a natural companion to Touch. It was adapted into an anime series in 2009.

How the story is divided

The first volume is the childhood prologue that ends with Wakaba's death. The rest takes place at Seishū Gakuen, where Kō and his friends are placed on a second team, the "prefab" team, and must beat the school's first team to prove themselves. The middle volumes follow their rise under a new coach and their attempts at the summer tournament. The final volumes are Kō's last summer, and the match that decides whether Wakaba's dream will come true.

Adaptations

SynergySP's anime (2009–2010) adapted the whole manga in 50 episodes. The manga won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 2009.

title: Mao
synopsis: A girl who survived the accident that killed her parents walks through a gate into Taishō-era Japan and meets a cursed exorcist. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11An 11 by its title: visionary (master 11), and therefore the signal.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Mao has run in Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday since 2019. Nanoka Kiba is a middle-school student who, years earlier, was the only survivor of an accident that killed her parents. Walking through an old shopping arcade, she passes through a gate and finds herself in Japan's Taishō era, a century in the past.

The story

There she meets Mao, an onmyōji, a practitioner of exorcism and divination, who has lived for centuries under the curse of a cat demon. He tells her that she is not quite human either. Moving between the two eras, Nanoka helps him hunt the cat demon and uncover what happened to both of them.

The style

It is darker and more of a mystery than most of Takahashi's work. Its yōkai, curses and fights recall Inuyasha, while its dry humour and slow-burning relationships are unmistakably hers.

Why it matters

It shows one of manga's greatest storytellers still working at full strength, more than forty years after Urusei Yatsura.

How the story is divided

The series moves slowly between the two eras. In the Taishō past, Mao and his shikigami, Otoya, hunt the cat demon Byōki and investigate the deaths that followed his master's succession; in the present, Nanoka searches for the truth about her own accident. Mao's fellow disciples, rivals for their master's legacy, appear one by one, each with a reason to want him dead.

Adaptations

Sunrise's anime aired on NHK from April to September 2026, in 26 episodes.

Reading it today

Still running, with 31 volumes by October 2026. Readers who loved Inuyasha will find a quieter, more mysterious relative. Our entry on Rumiko Takahashi covers her other series.

title: The Heroic Legend of Arslan
synopsis: Hiromu Arakawa's adaptation of Yoshiki Tanaka's novels, about a gentle young prince who must win back his fallen kingdom. 116 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Reduced, this title gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

What it is

Hiromu Arakawa's The Heroic Legend of Arslan has run in Kodansha's Bessatsu Shōnen Magazine since 2013. It adapts Yoshiki Tanaka's fantasy novels, set in Pars, a kingdom inspired by ancient Persia.

The story

Arslan is the fourteen-year-old crown prince, kind, thoughtful and seen as weak by his stern father, King Andragoras. When the army of Pars is betrayed and destroyed by invaders from Lusitania, Arslan escapes with the loyal knight Daryun. They gather a small band, including the strategist Narsus, and set out to retake the kingdom.

The themes

The story asks what makes a good king. Arslan cannot outfight his enemies, but he listens, earns loyalty and questions Pars' own slavery. Battles are won by strategy as much as by swords.

Why it matters

It brings Arakawa's clear storytelling and strong characters, known from Fullmetal Alchemist, to a classic Japanese fantasy epic. It was adapted into an anime series in 2015.

The source novels

Yoshiki Tanaka's sixteen novels were published between 1986 and 2017. They follow Arslan's war to free Pars and, in a second, darker part, what happens after he becomes king. An earlier manga adaptation by Chisato Nakamura appeared in the 1990s, alongside anime films and video releases. Arakawa's adaptation follows the novels closely and adds her own character comedy.

Adaptations

Arakawa's manga was adapted as an anime in 2015, with a short second season, Dust Storm Dance, in 2016. Readers who know Arakawa from Fullmetal Alchemist will recognise her clear battle staging and her warmth towards ensemble casts; our guide to where to start with Hiromu Arakawa puts it in the context of her other work.

title: Happy!
synopsis: A teenage girl left with her brother's enormous debt to gangsters sets out to pay it off by becoming a professional tennis player. 30 in the letters, reducing to 3.
body:
3Title sums to 30 and reduces to 3 — The Telling, where the reference files an act of telling.

What it is

Naoki Urasawa's Happy! ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1993 to 1999 and was collected in twenty-three volumes. Miyuki Umino is a cheerful, orphaned high-school student who looks after her younger siblings. When her older brother runs off, he leaves her with a huge debt to a loan shark.

The story

Refusing the shady ways out she is offered, Miyuki decides to pay the debt by turning professional at tennis, a sport she played as a girl. She faces wealthy rivals who scheme against her, a hostile press and the snobbery of a sport for the rich, as well as a romance that keeps going wrong.

The style

It is an underdog sports drama played with comedy and melodrama, and in some ways Urasawa's tennis answer to his judo series Yawara!. Its villains are wonderfully nasty, and Miyuki's endurance is the point.

Why it matters

It was written in the same years Urasawa was drawing Monster, and shows the lighter, popular side of a creator now best known for thrillers.

How the story is divided

The first volumes follow Miyuki's decision to turn professional and her first matches, under the cheap and desperate coaching of a former player. Her great enemy is Chōko Ryūgasaki, a rich, beautiful player who plots against her and spreads rumours about her debts. The story builds through tournaments in Japan and abroad to Wimbledon, with a romance that Chōko is determined to wreck running alongside.

Adaptations

It was adapted for live-action television in the 2000s.

Reading it today

Complete in 23 volumes. Readers who enjoy it should read Yawara!, Urasawa's judo series, which works in the same way. Our entry on Naoki Urasawa covers his thrillers.

title: Inuyashiki
synopsis: A frail, ignored old man and a teenage boy are both rebuilt as machines by an alien accident; one uses the power to save lives, the other to take them. 54 in the letters, reducing to 9.
body:
9Reduced, this title gives 9. It sits on The Closing with the rest of a completion.

What it is

Hiroya Oku's Inuyashiki ran in Kodansha's Evening from 2014 to 2017 and was collected in ten volumes. Ichirō Inuyashiki is fifty-eight, looks much older and is ignored by his wife and children. Then his doctor tells him he has terminal cancer.

The story

That night, in a park, he is killed by a crashing alien craft, and rebuilt as a machine with enormous powers that look exactly like his old body. A high-school boy, Hiro Shishigami, was caught in the same accident. Inuyashiki discovers he can heal people and finally feels alive. Hiro, cold and alienated, starts killing.

The style

Oku's art mixes photographic backgrounds with brutal, detailed action, as in Gantz. But the core of the book is the contrast between a weak old man who becomes a hero and a boy who becomes a monster.

Why it matters

It is an unusual superhero story whose hero is an old man, and a dark look at loneliness, family and power. It was adapted into an anime in 2017 and a live-action film in 2018.

How the story is divided

The first volumes run two stories side by side: Inuyashiki discovering his powers and using them to heal and rescue people, and Hiro beginning to kill. Their paths cross when Hiro's identity is exposed and he declares war on Japan. The final volumes turn to a disaster on a world scale, and to Inuyashiki's last choice as a hero.

Adaptations

MAPPA's anime (2017) adapted the whole manga in eleven episodes, and a live-action film directed by Shinsuke Sato followed in 2018.

Reading it today

Complete in ten volumes, it is a short read, and a good way into Oku's work for readers who find Gantz too long.

title: Historie
synopsis: The life of Eumenes, secretary to Alexander the Great, from his childhood as a slave to the courts of Macedon. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4Filed under 4. The Structure takes a structure, and this entry is holds one.

What it is

Hitoshi Iwaaki's Historie has run in Kodansha's Afternoon since 2003, at a very slow pace. It follows Eumenes of Cardia, a real figure who became secretary to Philip II of Macedon and later served Alexander the Great.

The story

Eumenes grows up as the son of a wealthy family in the Greek city of Cardia, until he learns that he is of Scythian birth and is sold into slavery. He escapes, lives among villagers on the Black Sea coast and uses his wits, learning and coolness to survive, until fate brings him to Macedon.

The style

Iwaaki, the creator of Parasyte, draws with clean lines and calm, sudden violence. Eumenes is clever, detached and endlessly curious, and the series is full of humour, strategy and sharp observations about war and culture.

Why it matters

Little is recorded of Eumenes before he enters Macedonian service, and Iwaaki fills that gap with invention while staying inside what the sources allow. It won the Grand Prize of the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize in 2012.

How the story is divided

The early volumes are the story of Eumenes' youth, told as a flashback within his journey home to Cardia: his discovery of his Scythian origin, his enslavement, and his years in a village of Paphlagonia. The middle volumes bring him to Macedon, where he becomes Philip's secretary, and to the young Alexander, whom Iwaaki gives a second, violent personality named Hephaestion. The latest volumes follow Philip's wars in Greece.

Publication

New chapters appear rarely. The twelfth volume came out in June 2024, and the series won the Kodansha Manga Award in 2025, adding to its Japan Media Arts and Tezuka grand prizes. Liden Films' anime is scheduled for January 2027.

Reading it today

Twelve volumes. Our entry on Parasyte covers Iwaaki's best-known series, and our guide to manga set in history outside Japan places it among its peers.

title: Sunny
synopsis: Children in a foster home escape into an old broken-down car in the yard, in Taiyō Matsumoto's gentle, personal portrait of childhood. Read from the telling, as a 3.
body:
3A 3 by its title: creative communicator, and therefore the telling.

What it is

Taiyō Matsumoto's Sunny began in Shogakukan's IKKI in 2010 and was completed in six volumes. It is set in a children's home in 1970s Japan, where children live who cannot, for now, live with their parents.

The story

In the yard sits an old Nissan Sunny that no longer runs. For the children it is a spaceship, a hiding place, a getaway car and a place to be alone. Each chapter follows a different child: the newcomer Sei, who believes his mother will come back; the wild, grinning Haruo; and the others, waiting for visits that may never happen.

The style

Matsumoto's loose, scratchy line and soft watercolours show the world at a child's height. Nothing dramatic happens; the series is about small moments, longing and how children make their own escapes.

Why it matters

Matsumoto has said the story draws on his own childhood in a children's home. It is one of his most personal and moving works, and a fine introduction to his art beyond Ping Pong and Tekkonkinkreet.

How it is organised

There is no central plot. The children's home, called Hoshi no Ko, "Stars' Children", and its staff are the frame, and chapters follow its children in turn: Sei's visits to his mother, Haruo's fights and fantasies, and the younger children's games. The car in the yard is the place where each of them goes when the waiting becomes too much, and the series ends without solving anyone's life.

Reading it today

Complete in six volumes. Viz's English edition reproduces the colour pages, which are an important part of the experience. Our entry on Taiyō Matsumoto covers his other work.

title: Antique Bakery
synopsis: Four very different men run a late-night cake shop in Tokyo, in Fumi Yoshinaga's comedy of pastry, secrets and past wounds. Filed under 5, the turn.
body:
5The letters of this title total 59, a 5 — the number of freedom, disruption, and restless movement.

What it is

Fumi Yoshinaga's Antique Bakery ran in Shinshokan's Wings from 1999 to 2002 and was collected in four volumes. Keiichirō Tachibana, a wealthy former salaryman who does not even like sweets, opens a European cake shop called Antique in a quiet Tokyo neighbourhood.

The staff

His pastry chef, Yūsuke Ono, is a genius whose charm works on every man he meets, which has cost him every job he has had. Ex-boxer Eiji Kanda joins as an apprentice because he loves cake, and Tachibana's devoted family bodyguard, Chikage, becomes a waiter.

The tone

Most of it is light comedy, built on the customers' stories and loving descriptions of cakes. Underneath is something darker: Tachibana was kidnapped as a child, and his memory of it shapes the whole series.

Why it matters

It was one of the works that made Yoshinaga's name, and it shows her talents early: sharp dialogue, food drawn with love and quiet treatment of gay characters. It was adapted for Japanese television and as a Korean film.

How it is organised

Most chapters follow a customer, a cake and a small story. Between them, the staff's own stories unfold: Ono's past, Eiji's change from boxer to baker, and above all the slow solving of Tachibana's kidnapping, which comes to a head in the last volume.

Adaptations

A Fuji TV drama aired in 2001, Nippon Animation's anime in 2008, and the Korean film Antique in 2008.

Complete in four volumes. Our guide to manga about food and cooking places it among other food stories, and our entry on Fumi Yoshinaga covers her later work.

title: Gokinjo Monogatari
synopsis: An art-school student who dreams of her own fashion brand and the boy next door, in the series that leads into Paradise Kiss. Read from the turn, as a 5.
body:
5A 5 by its title: freedom seeker, and therefore the turn.

What it is

Ai Yazawa's Gokinjo Monogatari, "Neighbourhood Story", ran in Shueisha's Ribon from 1995 to 1998 and was collected in seven volumes. Mikako Kōda is a fashion-obsessed student at Yazawa Art School who wants to start her own clothing brand.

The story

Mikako lives in the same apartment block as Tsutomu Yamaguchi, her childhood friend, a handsome classmate who plays in a band. Over the series their friendship turns into love, while their friends at school find their own creative paths and loves.

The style

Yazawa's art is stylish and full of clothes, with collage-like pages and fashion drawn with real care. Its characters are art students trying to become themselves, not just to find a boyfriend.

Why it matters

It was a big hit in Ribon, and its world continues in Yazawa's Paradise Kiss, where Mikako's brand Happy Berry appears and her younger sister, Miwako, is one of the main characters. Together the two series show Yazawa's lifelong love of fashion.

How the story is divided

The story follows a year or so at Yazawa Art School. The first half is Mikako and Tsutomu's slow move from neighbours and friends to a couple, with Mikako's jealousy and her first steps as a designer. The second half shifts to the people around them: their friends at school, with their own loves and ambitions, and the troubles of a young couple whose futures may take them in different directions.

Adaptations

Toei's anime ran in 1995 and 1996, followed by a short film.

title: Level E
synopsis: An alien prince of genius intelligence and endless boredom plays elaborate pranks on Earth, in Yoshihiro Togashi's strange science-fiction comedy. Filed under 7, the inquiry.
body:
7Reduced, this title gives 7. It sits on The Inquiry with the rest of an open question.

What it is

Yoshihiro Togashi's Level E ran in Shueisha's Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1995 to 1997, between YuYu Hakusho and Hunter × Hunter, and was collected in three volumes. Earth, it turns out, is home to many aliens living in secret.

The story

A high-school baseball player, Yukitaka Tsutsui, moves into a new apartment and finds a strange young man already living there. He is the crown prince of the planet Dogra: a genius, beautiful, and so bored that he spends his time on Earth inventing cruel, brilliant pranks, while his long-suffering bodyguard, Captain Kraft, tries to keep him alive.

The style

It is a series of short stories rather than one long plot. Its tone shifts from comedy to horror to science fiction to parody, including a famous send-up of sentai heroes.

Why it matters

It shows Togashi's playful, clever side and his love of twisting genres. It was adapted into an anime in 2011.

How the story is divided

There are several separate stories, each a few chapters long. The first introduces the prince and Tsutsui and the aliens hiding in Yamagata Prefecture. Another, the best known, turns a group of middle-school children into a sentai team against their will, fighting monsters the prince has arranged for them. Others turn to horror, mystery and romance, and the last turns to the prince's own marriage.

Adaptations

Pierrot and David Production's anime (2011) adapted the whole manga in 13 episodes.

Reading it today

Complete in three volumes, it can be read in an evening. Our entry on Yoshihiro Togashi covers his other work.

title: Mazinger Z
synopsis: A boy inherits a giant robot from his grandfather and pilots it against an evil scientist, in the series that created the piloted super robot. Filed under 11, the signal.
body:
11Title sums to 56 and reduces to 11 — The Signal, where the reference files a signal received early.

What it is

Go Nagai's Mazinger Z began in Shueisha's Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1972, alongside its television anime by Toei. Kōji Kabuto is a hot-headed teenager whose grandfather, the scientist Jūzō Kabuto, has secretly built a giant robot of an indestructible alloy.

The story

Before he is killed by the agents of the evil Dr. Hell, who wants to conquer the world with an army of mechanical monsters, Kabuto leaves the robot to Kōji. Kōji pilots Mazinger Z from a small flying craft that docks in its head, and fights Dr. Hell's monsters one after another.

The new idea

Earlier giant robots, like Mitsuteru Yokoyama's Tetsujin 28-go, were operated by remote control. Nagai has said the idea came to him watching drivers in a traffic jam: what if you could drive a robot like a car? Putting the hero inside the machine changed the genre.

Why it matters

It created the super robot genre, with its named attacks, monster-of-the-week battles and enormous toy line. Almost every mecha story that followed, from Gundam to Evangelion, starts from its idea.

How it is organised

The story is mostly a series of battles, as Dr. Hell sends his mechanical beasts against Mazinger Z, along with his commanders, the half-man, half-woman Baron Ashura and the headless Count Brocken. Kōji is supported by Sayaka Yumi and her own robot, Aphrodite A, and by the scientists of the Photon Power Laboratory. The final battle against Dr. Hell leads directly into the sequel, Great Mazinger, in which a new pilot takes over.

Adaptations

Toei's anime ran for 92 episodes from 1972 to 1974. It was followed by Great Mazinger and UFO Robo Grendizer, the remake Shin Mazinger (2009) and the film Mazinger Z: Infinity (2017). The anime was a huge hit in Italy, Spain and Latin America.

Reading it today

title: Toriko
synopsis: In an age where the world revolves around food, a giant gourmet hunter and a timid chef search for the rarest ingredients on Earth. 34 in the letters, reducing to 7.
body:
7Title sums to 34 and reduces to 7 — The Inquiry, where the reference files an open question.

What it is

Mitsutoshi Shimabukuro's Toriko ran in Shueisha's Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2008 to 2016 and was collected in forty-three volumes. It is set in the Gourmet Age, when the world's economy, politics and culture all revolve around the search for delicious food.

The story

Toriko is a Gourmet Hunter, a huge, cheerful man who tracks down and fights rare and dangerous creatures and plants to eat. With him is Komatsu, a small, nervous hotel chef with a gift for cooking any ingredient. Toriko is assembling his "full course", the perfect meal of his life, from appetiser to dessert.

The style

It is a battle manga whose prizes are meals. Its monsters are wildly inventive, its fights get ever bigger, and every chapter ends with something to eat, drawn with obvious delight.

Why it matters

It mixed battle shōnen and food manga in a way no one else had, and was a mainstay of Jump in its era. It was adapted into an anime from 2011 to 2014, including a crossover with One Piece.

How the story is divided

The early volumes are hunts: Toriko and Komatsu track down one legendary ingredient after another, and meet the other Heavenly Kings, the hunters Coco, Sunny and Zebra. The middle of the series follows Toriko's training and the war between the International Gourmet Organisation and the Gourmet Corporation, a criminal empire that hunts for profit, over GOD, the greatest ingredient of all. The last part moves into the Gourmet World, a vast and lethal continent beyond the human world, and reveals what lies behind the Gourmet Age itself.

Adaptations

Toei's anime ran for 147 episodes from 2011 to 2014, with crossover episodes with One Piece and Dragon Ball Z.

title: Tokyo Revengers
altTitles: 東京卍リベンジャーズ
synopsis: A failing young man is thrown back twelve years to his delinquent middle-school days, and must change a gang's history to save his first girlfriend. 73 in the letters, reducing to 1.
body:
1Title sums to 73 and reduces to 1 — The Opening, where the reference files a first move.

What it is

Ken Wakui's Tokyo Revengers ran in Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine from 2017 to 2022 and was collected in thirty-one volumes. Takemichi Hanagaki is twenty-six, stuck in a dead-end job and convinced his life peaked in middle school. Then he learns that his only girlfriend, Hinata Tachibana, has been killed in a fight involving the Tokyo Manji Gang.

The story

Pushed from a station platform, Takemichi suddenly finds himself twelve years in the past, back as a middle-school delinquent. He discovers he can travel between the two times, and sets out to change the history of the Tokyo Manji Gang, led by the charismatic Mikey, so that Hinata will live.

How it works

The series mixes a time-travel thriller with a classic delinquent story of gangs, loyalty and fistfights. Each change Takemichi makes creates new and often worse futures, and he cannot fight well: he wins by never giving up.

Why it matters

It was one of the biggest manga of the early 2020s, especially after its 2021 anime and live-action film, and it brought the old delinquent genre back to a new generation.

How the story is divided

Each arc is a crisis in the history of the Tokyo Manji Gang that Takemichi has to change: the fight with Moebius on 3 August, the Bloody Halloween battle against Valhalla, the Christmas showdown with the Black Dragons, and the war with Tenjiku that ends Toman's first era. The last arcs jump forward to Mikey's later gang and to the final battle over his future, as the series reveals why the time leaps work at all.

Adaptations

The anime began in 2021 and continued with the Christmas Showdown and Tenjiku arcs in 2023, adapting the manga closely. The live-action film (2021) was a hit, and a two-part sequel covering Bloody Halloween followed in 2023. The series ends in 2022 after 278 chapters, and Wakui's earlier gang manga, Shinjuku Swan, about scouts in Kabukichō, was also adapted for film.

title: Rin-ne
synopsis: A girl who can see ghosts teams up with a broke, part-shinigami classmate who guides lingering spirits to the next world. The title reduces to 33 — the teaching.
body:
33Thirty-three — service. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Rin-ne ran in Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 2009 to 2017 and was collected in forty volumes. As a small child, Sakura Mamiya vanished for a while and came back able to see ghosts, which she treats with complete calm.

The story

In high school she meets Rinne Rokudō, a classmate who is part shinigami, a death god. His job is to send restless spirits on to reincarnation. But he is desperately poor, because the tools of his trade cost money, and his con-artist father keeps running up debts in his name.

The style

It is a gentle, episodic comedy. Each chapter brings a new ghost with a small, often silly reason for staying on Earth, and Rinne's poverty is a running joke. Romance moves very slowly, in Takahashi's familiar way.

Why it matters

It shows Takahashi in her relaxed, comic mode, between Inuyasha and Mao. It was adapted into three seasons of anime from 2015 to 2017.

How it is organised

Nearly every chapter is a self-contained ghost story, and the series is built on recurring characters rather than arcs: Rokumon, Rinne's contracted black cat; Tsubasa Jūmonji, an exorcist who loves Sakura; Ageha, a rival shinigami who loves Rinne; and Sabato, Rinne's father, whose cons fill the Damashigami Company with debt. Sakura's calm and Rinne's poverty drive most of the jokes, and the slow romance between them moves forward only in small steps until the end.

Adaptations

Brain's Base's anime ran for three seasons from 2015 to 2017.

Reading it today

Complete in 40 volumes, it can be read a few chapters at a time and in any order. Our entry on Rumiko Takahashi covers her longer stories.

title: Chobits
synopsis: A struggling student finds a discarded humanoid computer in the rubbish, and begins to wonder whether a machine can love. Filed under 4, the structure.
body:
4The letters of this title total 31, a 4 — the number of structure, labour, and the building of lasting systems.

What it is

CLAMP's Chobits ran in Kodansha's Young Magazine from 2000 to 2002 and was collected in eight volumes. In its near future, people own persocoms: personal computers built in the shape of beautiful humans.

The story

Hideki Motosuwa has failed his university entrance exams and moved to Tokyo to study for another try. Too poor to buy a persocom, he finds one thrown out with the rubbish, takes her home and switches her on. She knows only one word, "chi", which becomes her name, and she seems to be no ordinary model.

The themes

It begins as a comedy for young men, but it becomes a serious story about loneliness and what love means between a person and a machine. Chi reads a picture book that tells her own story in parallel.

Why it matters

It was one of CLAMP's biggest hits. It was adapted into an anime in 2002, and Chi later appeared in Tsubasa: Reservoir Chronicle.

How the story is divided

The first volumes are a comedy of Hideki teaching Chi to speak, read and shop, and his friends' troubles with their own persocoms. As the story goes on, it reveals that Chi may be one of the legendary Chobits, persocoms said to have real feelings, and the picture book she reads, A City with No People, begins to tell her own story. The final volumes reveal who built her and why, and ask Hideki whether he can love someone who cannot love in the way a human does.

Madhouse's anime (2002) adapted the whole manga in 26 episodes.

Complete in eight volumes, it is a quick read. Its questions about loving a machine feel more current now than when it was written, and CLAMP's Angelic Layer shares characters with it.

title: Tsubasa: Reservoir Chronicle
synopsis: A young archaeologist travels between worlds to recover the scattered memories of his princess, meeting characters from across CLAMP's work. The title reduces to 11 — the signal.
body:
11Filed under 11. The Signal takes a signal received early, and this entry is sees one.

What it is

CLAMP's Tsubasa: Reservoir Chronicle ran in Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine from 2003 to 2009 and was collected in twenty-eight volumes. In the desert kingdom of Clow, Princess Sakura and the young archaeologist Syaoran love each other. When her memories are scattered across other worlds as feathers, she is left close to death.

The story

Syaoran goes to the Dimensional Witch, Yūko, who grants wishes for a price. In exchange for the ability to travel between worlds, he must give up Sakura's memories of him. Two others join him for their own reasons, the ninja Kurogane and the magician Fai, and with the creature Mokona they leap from world to world.

A crossover

The worlds they visit are full of characters from CLAMP's other series, often in new roles: Cardcaptor Sakura's Sakura and Syaoran themselves, figures from Chobits, Magic Knight Rayearth and many more. It ran in parallel with xxxHolic, and the two stories cross repeatedly.

Why it matters

It is CLAMP's grandest crossover, and its later volumes turn into a complex story about identity, time and sacrifice. It was adapted into an anime in 2005.

How the story is divided

The first half is a journey from world to world, each a few chapters long, in which the group recovers one of Sakura's feathers. The Tokyo arc, in a ruined, rainless Tokyo, marks the turn: the story reveals that Syaoran himself is not what he seems, and the second half becomes a story about clones, copies and the man who planned the whole journey, Fei Wong Reed, before ending in the worlds of Clow and Japan where it began.

Adaptations

Bee Train's anime ran for two seasons in 2005 and 2006 and stops before the Tokyo arc. The OVAs Tokyo Revelations (2007) and Shunraiki (2009) adapt parts of the later story, and a film appeared in 2005. A sequel manga, Tsubasa: World Chronicle, followed from 2014 to 2016.

Reading it today

Complete in 28 volumes, and best read alongside xxxHolic, since the two stories explain each other.

title: Our Little Sister
synopsis: Three sisters living in Kamakura meet their teenage half-sister at their father's funeral and invite her to live with them. Filed under 6, the care.
body:
6Title sums to 69 and reduces to 6 — The Care, where the reference files an obligation.

What it is

Akimi Yoshida's Our Little Sister, known in Japan as Umimachi Diary, ran in Shogakukan's Flowers from 2006 to 2018 and was collected in nine volumes. The Kōda sisters, Sachi, Yoshino and Chika, live together in an old house in Kamakura. Their father left the family years before.

The story

When he dies, they go to his funeral and meet Suzu, their thirteen-year-old half-sister, who nursed him through his final illness. Sachi asks her to come and live with them in Kamakura, and she does. The series follows the four sisters through school, work, love and the town's seasons.

The style

It is a quiet family drama about grief, forgiveness and growing up. Yoshida shows Kamakura's streets, beaches and food in loving detail, and each sister has her own stories and loves.

Why it matters

It is the opposite pole of Yoshida's thriller Banana Fish, and shows the same control applied to almost nothing happening. It won the Manga Taishō in 2013, and Hirokazu Kore-eda adapted it as the live-action film Our Little Sister in 2015.

How it is organised

Each chapter is a small episode, told by one of the four sisters: Suzu's football team and her first romance, Sachi's affair with a married doctor and her work at a hospice, Yoshino's career at a bank and her failing relationships, Chika's quiet love for the manager of a sports shop. A few threads run across the whole: the death of a local café owner, Suzu's relationship with her late father's memory, and the question of what the sisters owe to each other. It ends with each of them choosing her next step.

Adaptations

Hirokazu Kore-eda's film (2015) competed at Cannes and won several Japanese Academy Awards.

Reading it today

Complete in nine volumes. The story connects to Yoshida's earlier Lovers' Kiss, set in the same town. Our entry on Banana Fish covers Yoshida's best-known work.

title: Baoh
synopsis: A teenager implanted with a deadly parasite by a secret organisation escapes, and protects a psychic girl as the bio-weapon Baoh awakens in him. 17 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8The letters of this title total 17, an 8 — the number of money, authority, and the machinery of ambition.

What it is

Hirohiko Araki's Baoh ran in Shueisha's Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1984 to 1985 and was collected in two volumes. It was one of Araki's early serialisations in Jump, shortly before JoJo's Bizarre Adventure.

The story

Ikuro Hashizawa is a teenager taken by a secret organisation, Doress, and implanted with a parasite called Baoh. When he is in danger, it transforms him into a monstrous, unstoppable weapon. During a transfer he escapes, together with Sumire, a young girl with psychic powers whom the organisation also wants, and Doress sends its agents after them.

The style

It is a short, violent action story, full of body horror and odd powers. Its strange poses, sound effects and narrator's explanations already look like early JoJo.

Why it matters

It shows where Araki's style began, and it is a quick read for any JoJo fan. It was adapted into an original video animation in 1989.

How the story is divided

The story is short and straightforward: Ikuro and Sumire's escape from the Doress transport, their flight across Japan, and a series of encounters with the organisation's agents, each with a stranger power than the last. The last chapters are an assault on the Doress facility, as Baoh's power grows beyond what its creators planned.

Adaptations

Pierrot's OVA (1989) adapted the whole story in one episode.

Reading it today

Complete in two volumes. Readers who know JoJo can see the origins of Araki's body horror, his poses and his explanatory narration. Our entry on Hirohiko Araki covers his later career.

title: H2
synopsis: Two boyhood friends, a pitcher and a slugger, become rivals on the way to Kōshien, and between two girls, in Mitsuru Adachi's baseball classic. 8 in the letters, with nothing left to reduce.
body:
8Title sums to 8 with nothing to reduce — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

What it is

Mitsuru Adachi's H2 ran in Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1992 to 1999 and was collected in thirty-four volumes. Hiro Kunimi was a star pitcher in middle school until a doctor told him his elbow was ruined. He chose a high school with no baseball team.

The story

Then Hiro learns the diagnosis was wrong. He sets out to build a team from nothing, while his best friend, the great slugger Hideo Tachibana, plays for a powerful rival school. Between them is Hikari, Hiro's childhood friend and Hideo's girlfriend, and beside Hiro is Haruka, the cheerful team manager. The title's two H's stand for the two boys and the two girls.

The style

Like all of Adachi's work, it is understated and funny, with feelings carried in silences. The baseball is exciting, but the core is the friendship and the love that no one quite says.

Why it matters

It is one of Adachi's longest and most popular series, often ranked with Touch and Cross Game as his best. It became an anime in 1995 and a television drama in 2005.

How the story is divided

The first volumes follow Hiro's founding of a baseball club at Senkawa High and the battle to get it recognised. The middle of the series follows the team's rise through the summer and spring tournaments, while Hiro slowly realises his feelings for Hikari and Haruka grows closer to him. The last volumes are a summer Kōshien in which Hiro and Hideo finally face each other, and the match settles both the baseball and the romance.

Adaptations

The 1995 anime adapted the early volumes, and a television drama in 2005 adapted the whole story.

title: Codename: Sailor V
altTitles: コードネームはセーラーV
synopsis: A schoolgirl becomes the masked heroine Sailor V, in the series that came before Sailor Moon and led directly to it. 66 in the letters, reducing to 3.

What it is

Naoko Takeuchi's Codename: Sailor V began in Kodansha's RunRun in 1991, a few months before Sailor Moon, and continued until 1997. Minako Aino is a sporty, boy-crazy thirteen-year-old who loves video games.

The story

A white cat named Artemis tells Minako that she is the Champion of Justice, and gives her a magical pen that lets her transform into the masked heroine Sailor V. She fights the Dark Agency, a criminal organisation that uses the entertainment industry to steal people's energy, while becoming famous in Tokyo.

Its link to Sailor Moon

The series was so promising that a television anime was proposed. That proposal grew into Sailor Moon, in which Minako returns as Sailor Venus, one of Sailor Moon's guardians. The two series share their world, and Sailor V itself appears in Sailor Moon as a video game.

Why it matters

It is the origin of one of manga's most famous franchises, and a lighter, comic story in its own right.

How it is organised

Most chapters are self-contained comic adventures: Minako investigates an idol singer, a video game, a fan club or a film shoot, each a front for the Dark Agency. The series ended in 1997, shortly after Sailor Moon, with a last arc that connects Minako's story to her role as Sailor Venus.

Editions

It has been reissued in new editions alongside Sailor Moon. There is no separate anime, though Minako's history as Sailor V is woven into the Sailor Moon anime.

title: Land of the Lustrous
synopsis: Far in the future, living gems defend themselves against raiders from the moon, and the most fragile of them sets out to be useful. The title reduces to 5 — the turn.
body:
5Filed under 5. The Turn takes a turn, and this entry is changes one.

What it is

Haruko Ichikawa's Land of the Lustrous ran in Kodansha's Afternoon from 2012 to 2024. On a far-future Earth, humans are long gone. Twenty-eight immortal, gem-like beings live under the guidance of a monk-like teacher, Kongō-sensei.

The story

The Lunarians, beautiful beings who come down from the moon, raid them to shatter them and carry the pieces away. Phosphophyllite, the youngest and one of the softest gems, is too fragile to fight and is given the job of writing an encyclopedia. Phos wants to matter, and over the series is broken, rebuilt and transformed again and again.

The style

Ichikawa's art is spare and elegant, with lots of white space, glittering bodies and graceful action. It begins almost as a comedy, and turns into a profound, painful story about identity, faith and loss.

Why it matters

Its premise has no obvious precedent: immortal gem-people, a moon that hunts them, and a protagonist whose body is replaced piece by piece until the question of who is still there becomes the story. It ended in 2024 after twelve years, and its 2017 anime, made entirely in 3D computer animation by Orange, was widely praised.

How the story is divided

The early volumes follow Phos's search for a purpose: writing the encyclopedia, a journey into the sea, the loss of Phos's legs and their replacement with agate shells, and the loss of Phos's arms, replaced with gold alloy. As Phos grows stronger and stranger, Phos begins to question Kongō-sensei and travels to the moon. The second half divides the gems between the Earth and the moon, and the series ends in a way few readers predicted, on a scale of time far beyond human life.

Adaptations

Orange's 2017 anime covers only the early volumes. It has had no second season.

Reading it today

Complete in 13 volumes. Viewers of the anime can continue from where it ends, early in the story. The art rewards slow reading, and the ending repays a second look at the beginning.

title: Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic
synopsis: A boy magician with a djinn in his flute and a young adventurer raid magical dungeons, in a fantasy built from the Arabian Nights. 118 in the letters, reducing to 1.
body:
1Title sums to 118 and reduces to 1 — The Opening, where the reference files a first move.

What it is

Shinobu Ohtaka's Magi ran in Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 2009 to 2017 and was collected in thirty-seven volumes. Its world is built from the One Thousand and One Nights, with characters named after Aladdin, Alibaba, Sinbad and others.

The story

Aladdin is a cheerful, mysterious boy who carries a flute containing a giant djinn named Ugo. He befriends Alibaba, a young man who dreams of conquering a dungeon, one of the towers of treasure and magic that have appeared around the world. With Morgiana, a former slave of great strength, they are drawn into the politics of nations and a struggle over fate itself.

The themes

It starts as a light adventure and grows into a story about kingship, slavery, war and free will, with a whole world of rival empires.

Why it matters

It drew on the Thousand and One Nights rather than on the European models most fantasy manga use, borrowing Aladdin, Alibaba and Sinbad as its leads. It was adapted into anime from 2012 and spun off into Adventure of Sinbad, a prequel about the king who befriends the heroes.

How the story is divided

The series opens with a light adventure in the desert, as Aladdin and Alibaba conquer their first dungeon. It then moves to Balbadd, Alibaba's homeland, in a revolution against its corrupt king; to Sindria, the island kingdom of Sinbad; to the magic academy of Magnostadt, where Aladdin studies; and to a great war between the empires of Kou and Reim and the forces of Al-Thamen, the sorcerers who manipulate fate. The last arcs turn to Sinbad's own ambitions, and to a contest over whether people should choose their destinies.

Adaptations

A-1 Pictures' anime ran for two seasons, The Labyrinth of Magic (2012–2013) and The Kingdom of Magic (2013–2014), covering about half of the manga. Adventure of Sinbad was adapted in 2016.

title: Platinum End
synopsis: A suicidal teenager is saved by an angel and made one of thirteen candidates competing to become the new god, in the third work by the creators of Death Note. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:

What it is

Platinum End, written by Tsugumi Ohba and drawn by Takeshi Obata, ran in Shueisha's Jump SQ from 2015 to 2021 and was collected in fourteen volumes. Mirai Kakehashi is a teenager who has lost his family and been mistreated by the relatives who took him in. On the day he graduates from middle school, he jumps from a building.

The story

He is caught by an angel, Nasse, who has chosen him as one of thirteen candidates to replace God, who will retire in 999 days. Each candidate is given wings, red arrows that make anyone fall in love with them and, for some, white arrows that kill. Some candidates decide that the quickest way to become god is to murder the others.

The themes

Mirai wants only happiness and refuses to kill, which puts him against more ruthless rivals. The series asks about suicide, happiness, the existence of God and whether life has meaning, and its ending provoked strong debate.

Why it matters

It is the third collaboration by the team behind Death Note and Bakuman, and shows Obata's art at its most polished. It was adapted into an anime in 2021.

How the story is divided

The first volumes introduce the candidates and Mirai's alliance with Saki, another candidate who has thought of suicide. The middle of the series is a contest with Metropoliman, a candidate who hides behind a superhero costume and murders his rivals, and ends with his defeat. The last part turns to a public debate among the surviving candidates, in front of the world, about who should become God, before an ending on a scale few readers expected.

Adaptations

Signal.MD's anime ran from 2021 to 2022 and adapted the whole manga.
